question: Why is systematic site rotation clinically necessary for patients receiving daily subcutaneous injections?

options.A: It maintains predictable drug absorption and prevents tissue damage
options.B: It completely eliminates the sensation of pain during insertion
options.C: It stops the immune system from developing systemic allergies
options.D: It prevents the needle from becoming dull during repeated use

explanation: Healthy, undamaged tissue ensures proper drug uptake, whereas scarred or fatty tissue alters pharmacokinetics. [learn more](GNS125_U3_T7#GNS125_U3_T7_h5)

question: What is the primary skin layer targeted during an intradermal injection?

options.A: The dermis layer

question: Why is absorption significantly slower with intradermal injections?

options.A: Medications used are always oily suspensions
options.B: The needle depth blocks local circulation
options.C: The dermis has limited blood vessel supply
options.D: Skin cells in the dermis resist fluid

question: A Mantoux tuberculin skin test is administered via which route?

options.A: Intradermal route
options.B: Intravenous route
options.C: Subcutaneous route
options.D: Intramuscular route

question: A patient requires routine screening for tuberculosis exposure. Which action should the nurse take?

question: What is the maximum volume of medication typically given intradermally?

options.A: 0.5 mL
options.B: 1.0 mL

question: Which syringe type is standard for administering an intradermal injection?

question: What is the preferred anatomical site for a standard tuberculin skin test?

options.A: Lateral deltoid muscle region
options.B: Upper outer quadrant of the buttock

options.D: Anterior thigh muscle area

question: Why should a nurse avoid scarred skin areas when choosing an injection site?

options.A: Blood vessels in scars increase bleeding risk

options.C: Scar tissue alters absorption and obscures reactions

question: At what angle should the nurse insert the needle for an intradermal injection?

options.A: 60 to 75 degrees

question: Why is massaging the injection site discouraged after an intradermal injection?

question: What part of a tuberculin skin reaction is measured to determine a positive result?

question: A patient returns after 72 hours for a reading of their Mantoux test. What should the nurse assess?

question: What should the nurse do if no raised bleb appears during an intradermal injection?

question: Which complication is most associated with allergy skin testing?

question: What is the main benefit of giving medication directly into a joint space?

question: Why is keeping the area completely sterile so important during a joint injection?

options.A: Bacteria introduced into the joint space can cause septic arthritis

options.C: Joint cavities are prone to severe infections due to limited vascular supply
options.D: Unsterile technique immediately deactivates the administered steroid

question: Which type of drug is commonly injected into joints to bring down swelling and inflammation?

question: Viscosupplementation agents like hyaluronic acid are mostly used to manage which condition?

question: Which situation is a major reason NOT to perform a joint injection?

question: A patient scheduled for a knee joint injection takes warfarin. What should the nurse do first?

question: Which skin cleanser is most commonly used to prep the skin before a joint injection?

question: Why must skin antiseptic agents dry completely before the nurse inserts the needle?

options.C: To stop the patient from experiencing a burning sensation

question: What self-care advice is usually given to a patient right after a joint injection?

options.D: Massaging the injection site vigorously

question: What normal reaction can happen a few hours after a patient receives a joint steroid injection?

question: Which symptom helps a nurse tell the difference between a normal post-injection flare and septic arthritis?

question: A patient with diabetes notices high blood sugar readings at home after getting a joint steroid injection. What causes this?

options.B: Dietary indiscretion following the joint procedure
options.C: Inadequate skin preparation prior to the injection

question: What primary role does a nurse play in preventing drug errors?

question: System failures in medication safety usually involve which of the following?

options.D: Intentional harm caused by the medical staff

question: When should a nurse document that a medication was given?

question: Why must a nurse use two unique identifiers to check the right patient?

options.C: To check if the patient has health insurance

question: How should high-alert medications like narcotics be stored on the ward?

options.D: On top of the medication trolley in a basket

question: What is the main reason for using tall-man lettering on drug labels?

question: A patient is prescribed digoxin. What must the nurse check before giving this drug?

options.D: Respiratory rate

question: What is the primary purpose of checking patient allergies before drug administration?

options.C: To determine the patient's dietary food preferences
options.D: To calculate the correct financial bill for drugs

question: What practice must be avoided when preparing injectable medications?

question: Why is independent double-checking recommended for high-risk drug calculations?

question: Which type of tablet must never be crushed before administration?

question: Why must the nurse stay at the bedside until oral medications are swallowed?

question: What is the main purpose of post-administration monitoring?

question: How soon should a nurse monitor a patient after starting a new intravenous antibiotic?

question: What is the immediate priority when a medication error occurs?

options.B: Calling the pharmacy department to replace the drug

question: Why do hospitals use incident reports for medication mistakes?

question: What is the main purpose of enteric coating on certain oral medication tablets?

question: Which anatomical structure is the primary site for absorbing oral medications?

options.A: Small intestine
options.B: Large colon
options.C: Stomach lining
options.D: Esophagus

question: How does severe diarrhea typically affect the absorption of an oral prescription drug?

question: What is the biological term for the fraction of an administered drug that reaches systemic circulation unchanged?

question: Why does oral administration often result in lower drug concentration compared to intravenous administration?

question: A patient with a nasogastric tube needs an oral medication that is formulated as a sustained-release tablet. What is the appropriate nursing action?

question: Which nursing instruction is essential when administering an oral medication that binds to food in the stomach?

options.A: Mix the crushed tablet powder into dairy products to improve taste

options.C: Swallow the tablet immediately following a heavy, high-fat meal

explanation: Certain drugs interact with food components or require acid-free environments, making administration on an empty stomach necessary. [learn more](GNS125_U5_T1#GNS125_U5_T1_h7)

question: What four processes are included in the term drug disposition?

question: Why might a standard drug dose not work the same way for every patient?

question: Which kidney function consistently declines in older adults and affects how drugs leave the body?

options.A: Bladder detrusor tone

question: An increase in body fat in older adults changes how which type of drug is stored in the body?

options.A: Inorganic mineral salts
options.B: Protein-bound electrolytes
options.C: Lipid-soluble medications
options.D: Water-soluble medications

question: Grapefruit juice interacts with certain medications by blocking which specific enzyme in the gut?

question: Why does severe protein malnutrition increase the risk of drug toxicity for medications that bind to proteins in the blood?

options.A: It causes rapid renal elimination of the primary active metabolite

options.C: There are higher levels of free, unbound active drug floating in the bloodstream

explanation: Low albumin levels mean fewer binding sites exist, leaving a larger fraction of free drug active and available to cause toxicity. [learn more](GNS125_U5_T10#GNS125_U5_T10_h3)

question: Long-term exposure to industrial toxins in the workplace primarily alters how the body handles drugs by affecting which organ?

options.A: Liver
options.B: Pancreas
options.C: Spleen
options.D: Thyroid

explanation: The liver houses the primary metabolic enzymes responsible for processing xenobodies and toxins, making it the main organ affected by occupational exposures. [learn more](GNS125_U5_T10#GNS125_U5_T10_h4)

question: How does liver enzyme induction from industrial chemical exposure typically affect a patient's prescription drug needs?

options.A: Lower doses are required to prevent immediate kidney failure
options.B: Higher doses may be needed because the body clears the drug faster
options.C: Medications must be given exclusively through an IV line
options.D: Dosing remains unchanged because toxins do not affect pharmacokinetics

explanation: Upregulated liver enzymes break down medications more quickly, which can drop plasma levels below the therapeutic window. [learn more](GNS125_U5_T10#GNS125_U5_T10_h4)

question: What is the main effect of severe liver cirrhosis on how the body clears medications?

options.A: Immediate conversion of all drugs into inactive salts
options.B: Accelerated excretion through the biliary duct system
options.C: Decreased metabolism leading to drug buildup in the body
options.D: Complete elimination of first-pass gastrointestinal losses

explanation: Cirrhosis damages hepatic tissue and reduces enzyme production, which slows down metabolism and allows drugs to accumulate. [learn more](GNS125_U5_T10#GNS125_U5_T10_h5)

question: Why can a severe infection with high systemic inflammation change how a patient responds to medications?

options.A: Fever increases the rate of kidney filtration beyond normal limits
options.B: White blood cells actively bind to free drug molecules in the blood
options.C: Inflammatory signals slow down liver enzyme activity

question: Which lab values should a nurse check to assess a patient's ability to metabolize drugs?

options.A: Liver enzymes

question: A nurse reviews a new prescription for an elderly patient with kidney problems. What is the best initial nursing action?

options.A: Administer the medication with a large glass of grapefruit juice

options.D: Instruct the patient to double the dose if symptoms do not improve

explanation: Elderly patients with kidney impairment often require adjusted doses to prevent drug accumulation and toxicity. [learn more](GNS125_U5_T10#GNS125_U5_T10_h6)

question: What is drug distribution defined as in pharmacokinetics?

options.A: The permanent breakdown of active drug molecules in the liver
options.B: The reversible transfer of a drug between body compartments
options.C: The complete elimination of waste products through the kidneys
options.D: The rate at which a tablet dissolves in the stomach

question: Why do fat-soluble drugs move quickly out of the bloodstream?

options.A: They repel water molecules in the body fluids

question: Which feature in standard blood vessels allows water-soluble drugs to leave the circulation?

options.A: Active energy pumps
options.B: Thick skin layers
options.C: Tiny pores between cells
options.D: Solid vessel walls

question: What makes it hard for a drug to cross strict barriers in the body?

options.A: Small size and high fat solubility
options.B: Large size and high water solubility
options.C: Strong attraction to red blood cells
options.D: Quick breakdown by blood enzymes

explanation: Large or water-soluble molecules cannot easily slip through tight cellular junctions without special transport. [learn more](GNS125_U5_T2#GNS125_U5_T2_h2)

question: Which main blood protein is primarily responsible for binding acidic drugs?

options.A: Fibrinogen
options.B: Albumin
options.C: Hemoglobin

explanation: Albumin is the main circulating plasma protein that binds acidic and neutral drug molecules in the bloodstream. [learn more](GNS125_U5_T2#GNS125_U5_T2_h3)

question: What does a very high volume of distribution tell you about a drug?

options.A: It binds permanently to red blood cells
options.B: It spreads heavily into body tissues
options.C: It leaves the body immediately through urine
options.D: It stays strictly inside the blood plasma

question: Why might a doctor order a larger starting dose for a drug that spreads heavily into body tissues?

options.A: Most of the drug leaves the blood and goes into storage sites

options.C: The kidneys remove the entire dose too fast
options.D: The drug turns into crystals inside blood vessels

explanation: When a drug hides in tissues, a larger initial dose is needed to achieve effective therapeutic levels in the blood. [learn more](GNS125_U5_T2#GNS125_U5_T2_h4)

question: Which group of organs receives a drug the fastest right after it enters the bloodstream?

options.A: Skin, bones, and tendons
options.B: Fat tissue and resting skeletal muscle
options.C: Cartilage and joints
options.D: Brain, heart, liver, and kidneys

question: Why do fat-soluble drugs tend to build up in body fat over time?

options.A: Fat tissue has low blood flow and stores fat-loving compounds well
options.B: Blood flow to fat is higher than to the brain
options.C: Fat cells pull drugs inward using active pumps
options.D: Fat tissue turns the drug into solid crystals

question: What feature of the blood-brain barrier stops water-soluble drugs from entering the brain?

question: What is the main concern when a pregnant woman takes medications that cross the placenta?

question: How does severe malnutrition affect how drugs behave in the body?

options.A: Dehydration greatly expands total body fluid volume

question: A dehydrated child with severe diarrhea gets a standard dose of a water-soluble antibiotic. What is the likely result of having less fluid in the body?

question: Why might a fat-soluble drug that spreads widely through the body stay active for a long time?

question: An older adult with changes in body fat is given a fat-soluble sedative. What should the nurse watch out for?

question: What is the main goal of drug metabolism in the body?

question: How does a prodrug differ from a standard active drug?

question: Which organ is the main site for drug metabolism?

question: Besides the liver, which other part of the body plays a big role in breaking down drugs before they enter general circulation?

question: What is the main chemical result of a Phase I metabolic reaction?

question: Where are Cytochrome P450 enzymes mostly found inside liver cells?

question: Why do genetic differences in CYP450 enzymes matter for patient care?

question: What happens when a patient takes an enzyme-inducing drug along with a regular medication?

question: What is it called when one drug blocks the metabolic enzyme activity of another drug?

question: What term describes the amount of an unchanged drug that actually reaches the general bloodstream?

question: Why do oral medications often need a higher dose than drugs given through a vein?

question: Which of these is NOT a reason why drug processing varies among different populations?

question: Why must nurses ask patients if they are taking traditional herbal remedies?

question: What is the primary organ responsible for eliminating water-soluble drugs from the body?

question: Why are gases like inhaled anesthetics mainly breathed out through the lungs?

question: Which type of drug molecules can pass through the kidney's tiny filtering units?

question: For a drug to stay trapped in the kidney tubes and be passed out in urine, what property must it have?

question: How does making a patient's urine more alkaline affect weak acid medications?

question: Why do older adults often need lower doses of drugs that are cleared by the kidneys?

options.C: Their active kidney secretion works much faster

question: Where do drugs that are excreted through the biliary system eventually end up?

question: What happens when a drug goes through enterohepatic recirculation in the body?

question: Which way of eliminating drugs from the body can pose a direct risk to a nursing infant?

question: Why does the alcohol in a person's breath match the level of alcohol in their blood?

question: What does a drug's half-life mean in clinical practice?

question: How does severe kidney failure affect a drug's elimination half-life?

options.C: It stops drug breakdown in the stomach entirely
options.D: It makes the half-life longer because the drug leaves the body slower

question: Which lab test do nurses usually check to see how well a patient's kidneys are clearing drugs?

question: Why do nurses closely monitor patients with kidney problems who are taking drugs cleared by the kidneys?

question: What is the primary focus of pharmacodynamics?

options.D: Hospital pharmacies refuse to stock medications for rare events

explanation: Because these reactions are unusual and varied, treatment focuses on supporting failing body organs while natural recovery happens. [learn more](GNS125_U5_T9#GNS125_U5_T9_h6)

question: Which agency in Nigeria is primarily responsible for receiving reports on adverse drug reactions?

options.A: FMOH
options.B: NAFDAC
options.C: NMCN
options.D: NCDC

explanation: NAFDAC handles pharmacovigilance and tracks adverse drug reactions nationwide in Nigeria. [learn more](GNS125_U5_T9#GNS125_U5_T9_h7)

question: Why is detailed charting of an unusual drug reaction in a patient's record so vital?

options.A: It guarantees the patient will never need any medication again
options.B: It prevents future healthcare providers from giving the dangerous drug again
options.C: It allows the hospital to bill the pharmaceutical company for damages
options.D: It proves the nurse followed every hospital protocol correctly

explanation: Clear charting ensures that everyone on the healthcare team knows the patient is dangerously sensitive to that specific drug. [learn more](GNS125_U5_T9#GNS125_U5_T9_h7)

question: What is the main focus of a National Drug Policy compared to a general health policy?

options.A: Pharmaceuticals and medicine supply chains
options.B: Medical doctor and nurse salary structures
options.C: Hospital building construction and maintenance
options.D: Global health donor funding negotiations

explanation: Think of it this way: while a general health policy looks at everything in healthcare, a National Drug Policy zooms in specifically on medicines—making sure they are produced, distributed, and used safely! [learn more](GNS215_U1_T1#GNS215_U1_T1_h1)

question: Why must a National Drug Policy tie in closely with the National Health Policy?

options.A: It allows pharmaceutical companies to set their own market prices without government interference.
options.B: International donors will refuse to release funds if the two policies are separate documents.
options.C: Medications are essential therapeutic tools required to achieve overall population health goals.
options.D: It prevents nurses from having to purchase hospital supplies out of their own pockets.

explanation: You can't achieve a healthy nation without medicines! Because drugs are our most common tool for treatment, the drug policy has to support the country's bigger health goals. [learn more](GNS215_U1_T1#GNS215_U1_T1_h1)

question: When did Nigeria introduce its first official National Drug Policy to fix chaotic drug distribution?
explanation: Nigeria rolled out its very first formal National Drug Policy back in 1990 to clean up unregulated drug imports and fight fake medicines. [learn more](GNS215_U1_T1#GNS215_U1_T1_h2)

question: What major problem pushed Nigeria to create its early drug policies?

options.A: A mandate from private pharmaceutical companies to raise drug prices
options.B: The widespread circulation of fake and adulterated drugs in open markets
options.C: The sudden surplus of locally manufactured vaccines and antibiotics
options.D: The complete absence of hospitals and clinics in rural communities

explanation: Open drug markets were flooded with fake and harmful products. This huge public health danger forced the government to step in with strict rules. [learn more](GNS215_U1_T1#GNS215_U1_T1_h2)

question: Which of these is a core pillar of the National Drug Policy?

options.A: Mandatory retirement age for pharmacists
options.B: Quality, safety, and efficacy of medicines
options.C: Privatization of all public teaching hospitals
options.D: Elimination of nursing schools in rural areas

explanation: Spot on! Making sure drugs are safe, work properly (efficacy), and are top quality is the heart of any good drug policy. [learn more](GNS215_U1_T1#GNS215_U1_T1_h3)

question: A clinic administrator is buying medications following the National Drug Policy. What should guide this choice?

options.A: Purchasing large quantities of single-use antibiotics regardless of disease patterns
options.B: Focusing on safety, efficacy, affordability, and availability of essential medicines
options.C: Stocking only medications that are heavily advertised on television and radio
options.D: Buying the most expensive imported brands to guarantee maximum patient prestige

explanation: When stocking a clinic, we always look for drugs that are safe, work well, patients can afford, and are actually available when needed! [learn more](GNS215_U1_T1#GNS215_U1_T1_h3)

question: Which agency is primarily responsible for regulating drugs in Nigeria?

options.A: NMA
options.B: FMOH
options.C: NAFDAC
options.D: NMNC

explanation: NAFDAC is our frontline agency charged with checking and controlling food, drugs, cosmetics, and medical devices across Nigeria. [learn more](GNS215_U1_T1#GNS215_U1_T1_h4)

question: Why must a nurse check for an official agency registration number on a drug before giving it?

options.A: To determine which pharmaceutical company manufactured the raw chemical compound
options.B: To calculate the exact wholesale profit margin for the hospital pharmacy
options.C: To ensure the medication qualifies for international shipping exemptions
options.D: To confirm that the drug has been evaluated for safety, quality, and efficacy

explanation: That registration number is your safety green light! It tells you NFDAC or the relevant body has tested the drug and approved it for use. [learn more](GNS215_U1_T1#GNS215_U1_T1_h4)

question: What is the main idea behind the Essential Medicines Concept?

options.A: The mandatory use of expensive imported brand-name drugs over generics
options.B: A select list of priority drugs that meet the healthcare needs of the majority
options.C: Stocking every single pharmaceutical formulation ever invented in every clinic
options.D: Allowing patients to dispense their own prescription drugs without guidance

explanation: Essential medicines are a carefully picked list of priority drugs that treat the most common health needs of everyday people effectively and cheaply. [learn more](GNS215_U1_T1#GNS215_U1_T1_h5)

question: Which of these clinical actions goes against the rules of rational drug use?

options.A: Prescribing strong broad-spectrum antibiotics for a simple viral upper respiratory infection
options.B: Educating a diabetic patient on the correct technique for self-administering insulin
options.C: Administering a standard dose of paracetamol for a documented fever in an adult
options.D: Checking a patient's kidney function before starting a new maintenance medication

explanation: Remember: antibiotics fight bacteria, not viruses! Giving them for a simple cold or viral infection wastes medicine and causes drug resistance. [learn more](GNS215_U1_T1#GNS215_U1_T1_h5)

question: What is the difference between substandard and counterfeit medications?

options.A: Substandard drugs are manufactured locally, while counterfeit drugs are always imported.
options.B: Counterfeit drugs are cheaper versions of safe generics produced by licensed companies.
options.C: Substandard drugs fail quality specifications, while counterfeit drugs are deliberately mislabeled copies.
options.D: Substandard drugs have expired dates, while counterfeit drugs contain too much active ingredient.

explanation: Substandard drugs are usually genuine products that missed quality marks, while counterfeits are fake, fraudulent copies made to deceive us. [learn more](GNS215_U1_T1#GNS215_U1_T1_h6)

question: A patient with severe malaria isn't getting better despite finishing a full course of drugs bought from an unverified roadside vendor. What should you suspect?

options.A: The patient requires an immediate surgical intervention for appendicitis.
options.B: The hospital ward is experiencing an outbreak of a normal bacterial infection.
options.C: The patient's body has suddenly developed a lifelong immunity to all fevers.
options.D: The medication administered may be substandard or counterfeit.

explanation: When a trusted drug completely fails to work—especially from a shady source—always suspect that it might be a fake or low-quality product. [learn more](GNS215_U1_T1#GNS215_U1_T1_h6)

question: What is a key way nurses support national drug policies right at the bedside?

options.A: Manufacturing basic intravenous fluids in the hospital ward kitchen
options.B: Monitoring patient responses and reporting adverse drug reactions
options.C: Issuing official manufacturing licenses to private pharmaceutical companies
options.D: Setting market retail prices for all imported prescription drugs

explanation: As bedside nurses, we watch patients closely after giving medications. Spotting and reporting side effects or bad reactions helps keep drug safety in check! [learn more](GNS215_U1_T1#GNS215_U1_T1_h7)

question: Why is the nurse's role so crucial for making a National Drug Policy work in real life?

options.A: Nurses are solely responsible for importing essential medicines from international manufacturers.
options.B: Nurses are the frontline professionals who handle, administer, and educate patients about medications daily.
options.C: Nurses hold the legal authority to shut down illegal open-air drug markets across the country.
options.D: Nurses write the legal statutes that govern pharmaceutical practice in government courts.

explanation: Policies are just paper until we put them into practice! Because nurses handle, give, and teach about drugs every day, our actions make the policy a success. [learn more](GNS215_U1_T1#GNS215_U1_T1_h7)

question: What is the primary purpose of essential drugs in a healthcare system?

options.A: To replace all traditional remedies in rural communities
options.B: To provide experimental treatments for rare chronic illnesses
options.C: To generate maximum revenue for local pharmaceutical companies
options.D: To satisfy the priority health care needs of the population

explanation: Essential drugs are specifically chosen because they target the most common and urgent health conditions affecting a community. [learn more](GNS215_U1_T2#GNS215_U1_T2_h1)

question: Why does limiting the number of available medicines improve a health system?

options.A: It completely eliminates the risk of patient allergic reactions
options.B: It forces doctors to prescribe only expensive imported brands
options.C: It guarantees that pharmaceutical companies stop manufacturing
options.D: It lowers costs and makes medicine supply easier to manage

explanation: Carrying fewer, well-tested drugs simplifies purchasing, storage, and distribution while keeping prices affordable. [learn more](GNS215_U1_T2#GNS215_U1_T2_h1)

question: In which year did the World Health Organization publish its first model list of essential medicines?
explanation: The World Health Organization introduced the very first model list in 1977 to help countries prioritize public health needs. [learn more](GNS215_U1_T2#GNS215_U1_T2_h2)

question: What major problem prompted the creation of the essential drugs concept?

options.A: Hospitals had too many doctors and not enough clinical space
options.B: Pharmaceutical companies refused to sell medicines to developing nations
options.C: Countries wasted money on redundant drugs while lacking basic treatments
options.D: Patients refused to take any form of modern pharmaceutical care

explanation: Early global health planners noticed limited budgets were being squandered on ineffective remedies instead of life-saving basics. [learn more](GNS215_U1_T2#GNS215_U1_T2_h2)

question: Which of the following is NOT a standard criterion for selecting an essential drug?

options.A: Bright packaging color and appealing flavor
options.B: High public health relevance
options.C: Proven clinical efficacy and safety
options.D: Acceptable cost-effectiveness

explanation: Aesthetic features like color and flavor do not determine whether a drug is medically essential for public health. [learn more](GNS215_U1_T2#GNS215_U1_T2_h3)

question: Why is cost-effectiveness a major factor when choosing essential drugs?

options.A: It guarantees that the manufacturer makes a high profit margin
options.B: It proves that the medicine was manufactured inside the country
options.C: It ensures limited financial resources can treat the maximum number of people
options.D: It eliminates the need for any healthcare workers to monitor patients

explanation: Because healthcare budgets are always restricted, choosing cost-effective options stretches funds to cover more patients in need. [learn more](GNS215_U1_T2#GNS215_U1_T2_h3)

question: How does bulk purchasing of essential drugs help health ministries?

options.A: It drives unit prices down and saves money
options.B: It increases the expiration rate of supplies
options.C: It complicates the daily work of pharmacists
options.D: It forces manufacturing companies to close down

explanation: Buying large quantities of standardized medicines allows governments to negotiate better prices and conserve funds. [learn more](GNS215_U1_T2#GNS215_U1_T2_h4)

question: What is a major clinical benefit for nurses and doctors who work with an essential drug list?

options.A: They can prescribe any experimental drug found anywhere in the world
options.B: They master a smaller group of drugs, leading to fewer prescription mistakes
options.C: They avoid communicating directly with patients about side effects
options.D: They never have to read medical journals or textbooks again

explanation: Knowing a concise list of reliable drugs helps clinicians understand dosages and interactions thoroughly, minimizing errors. [learn more](GNS215_U1_T2#GNS215_U1_T2_h4)

question: What is a common misconception patients sometimes hold about essential drugs?

options.A: They think essential drugs are only sold in overseas luxury clinics
options.B: They refuse to take them because they taste too sweet
options.C: They assume essential drugs can cure every known genetic disorder
options.D: They believe essential drugs are inferior because they are affordable

explanation: Because essential medicines are reasonably priced generics, some people wrongly assume they lack potency compared to expensive brands. [learn more](GNS215_U1_T2#GNS215_U1_T2_h5)

question: What administrative problem frequently disrupts the availability of essential medicines in clinics?

options.A: Too many pharmaceutical factories opening up in local towns
options.B: An excessive surplus of trained doctors in rural areas
options.C: Patients refusing to visit health facilities during dry seasons
options.D: Poor supply chain management and distribution bottlenecks

explanation: Even when drugs are budgeted for, weak logistics and transport systems often prevent them from reaching remote clinics on time. [learn more](GNS215_U1_T2#GNS215_U1_T2_h5)

question: What is a primary goal of incorporating essential drugs into Nigeria's national health strategy?

options.A: To restrict healthcare services only to urban federal capitals
options.B: To ensure affordable access to life-saving treatments like malaria medications
options.C: To eliminate all traditional medicine practices across every region
options.D: To promote the sale of expensive imported brand-name syrups

explanation: Nigeria's policy uses the essential medicines framework to guarantee that common deadly conditions like malaria have available treatments. [learn more](GNS215_U1_T2#GNS215_U1_T2_h6)

question: A rural health clinic in Nigeria runs out of basic antibiotics due to weak local distribution. Which national strategy is failing in this specific instance?

options.A: The regulation of surgical equipment manufacturing standards
options.B: The curriculum used to train primary school teachers
options.C: The Essential Drug Policy supply chain and distribution network
options.D: The enforcement of international luxury hotel taxation

explanation: Stockouts at rural clinics highlight flaws in the procurement and distribution mechanisms outlined by the national drug policy. [learn more](GNS215_U1_T2#GNS215_U1_T2_h6)

question: What is the main goal of the Essential Drug Programme?

options.A: To restrict patient access to common over-the-counter drugs
options.B: To make safe and effective medicines affordable and available
options.C: To eliminate the need for international pharmaceutical trade
options.D: To promote expensive brand-name pharmaceuticals in hospitals

explanation: You got this! The core idea is simple: making sure everyday life-saving medicines remain cheap enough and within reach for everyone who needs them. [learn more](GNS215_U1_T3#GNS215_U1_T3_h1)

question: Why does the Essential Drug Programme focus heavily on generic medicines instead of brand names?

options.A: Generics are generally much more affordable and optimize limited health budgets
options.B: Brand-name drugs are scientifically proven to be unsafe for public use
options.C: International law forbids developing nations from buying brand names
options.D: Generic medicines work faster in acute emergency conditions

explanation: Spot on! Generic drugs save money, helping clinics stretch tight budgets to treat more patients without cutting corners on quality. [learn more](GNS215_U1_T3#GNS215_U1_T3_h1)

question: When did the World Health Organization (WHO) publish its first Model List of Essential Medicines?
explanation: Great try! The WHO put out this very first list back in 1977 to bring order, safety, and priority to global drug markets. [learn more](GNS215_U1_T3#GNS215_U1_T3_h2)

question: What was the main problem in drug markets before the WHO introduced essential drug guidelines?

options.A: Patients refused to take any form of modern medical treatment
options.B: There were absolute shortages of chemical factories globally
options.C: Governments completely banned the importation of foreign drugs
options.D: Markets were flooded with too many unverified and expensive drug formulations

explanation: Well done! Back then, the market was chaotic with countless pricey products of doubtful quality, which confused doctors and drained wallets. [learn more](GNS215_U1_T3#GNS215_U1_T3_h2)

question: Which factor is most important when deciding if a medicine belongs on an essential drug list?

options.A: How recently the drug was invented in a laboratory
options.B: National disease prevalence and public health needs
options.C: The marketing budget of the manufacturing company
options.D: Whether the drug is packaged in a colorful container

explanation: Exactly! We pick drugs based on the actual illnesses that trouble our local communities the most. [learn more](GNS215_U1_T3#GNS215_U1_T3_h3)

question: A hospital committee is choosing between a brand-new, super expensive painkiller and an older, cheap one that works almost as well. What should they do?

options.A: Stock it only for patients who complain about older drugs
options.B: Buy large quantities to impress visiting health inspectors
options.C: Accept it immediately to stay modern and technologically advanced
options.D: Reject it because it fails the cost-effectiveness principle

explanation: You nailed it! As nurses and health planners, we always balance the health benefit against the cost to ensure wise spending. [learn more](GNS215_U1_T3#GNS215_U1_T3_h3)

question: What is a major benefit of having a standard list of medications in a clinic?

options.A: It guarantees that pharmaceutical companies make higher profits
options.B: It forces patients to buy medications outside the hospital
options.C: It reduces dispensing errors and simplifies inventory management
options.D: It completely eliminates the need for qualified pharmacists

explanation: That's right! Using a smaller, familiar group of drugs keeps storage organized and helps prevent medication mix-ups. [learn more](GNS215_U1_T3#GNS215_U1_T3_h4)

question: Which of these is NOT a standard rule when picking essential medicines?

options.A: Proven clinical effectiveness in human trials
options.B: Affordability for the target patient population
options.C: Safety compared to other choices
options.D: The aesthetic appeal of the product packaging

explanation: Correct! A pretty wrapper doesn't make a drug safer or more effective for our patients. [learn more](GNS215_U1_T3#GNS215_U1_T3_h4)

question: Which Nigerian agency works closely with the Ministry of Health to regulate and oversee drug standards?

options.A: NEMA
options.B: EFCC
options.C: NAFDAC
options.D: JAMB

explanation: You know this! NAFDAC is our frontline agency in Nigeria keeping fake and unsafe drugs away from our people. [learn more](GNS215_U1_T3#GNS215_U1_T3_h5)

question: Why does the National Essential Medicines List divide drugs by levels of healthcare (like PHCs vs teaching hospitals)?

options.A: To restrict advanced medical care exclusively to politicians and the wealthy
options.B: To match drug availability with the clinical competence and needs of each facility type
options.C: To ensure that primary health centers have the most expensive drugs first
options.D: To make record-keeping as difficult as possible for rural nurses

explanation: Spot on! Basic health centers stock what nurses can safely give, while complex specialist drugs go to advanced teaching hospitals. [learn more](GNS215_U1_T3#GNS215_U1_T3_h5)

question: What is a major danger when public clinics run out of basic medicines (stockouts)?

options.A: Hospitals automatically receive double their budget allocation
options.B: Doctors start prescribing fewer medications to save money
options.C: Pharmaceutical companies lower their international prices
options.D: Patients lose trust and may buy unsafe drugs from roadside vendors

explanation: Exactly. When shelves are empty, desperate patients turn to the street, exposing themselves to dangerous counterfeit drugs. [learn more](GNS215_U1_T3#GNS215_U1_T3_h6)

question: What procurement practice helps health authorities buy essential medicines at a much lower cost?

options.A: Bulk purchasing using generic non-proprietary names
options.B: Ordering exclusively through expensive luxury suppliers
options.C: Importing only patented brand-name formulations
options.D: Buying small batches from local retail pharmacies daily

explanation: Great job! Buying large quantities of generics lets health systems take advantage of bulk discounts. [learn more](GNS215_U1_T3#GNS215_U1_T3_h6)

question: What does 'rational drug use' mean for a patient?

options.A: Every patient leaves the clinic with at least five different prescriptions
options.B: Patients receive the right drug, correct dose, and proper duration for their condition
options.C: Doctors prescribe the most expensive medication available on the market
options.D: Pharmacies clear out all their expiring stock within forty-eight hours

explanation: You got it! Rational use means matching the exact illness with a safe, cost-effective treatment without waste or misuse. [learn more](GNS215_U1_T3#GNS215_U1_T3_h7)

question: Why is the overuse and misuse of antibiotics a serious public health threat?

options.A: It accelerates the development of dangerous antimicrobial resistance
options.B: It permanently ruins hospital refrigeration and storage units
options.C: It causes patients to develop allergic reactions to all known foods
options.D: It immediately bankrupts national pharmaceutical manufacturing firms

explanation: Spot on! Misusing antibiotics teaches bacteria how to survive them, creating superbugs that are terribly hard to treat later. [learn more](GNS215_U1_T3#GNS215_U1_T3_h7)

question: A patient tells you they plan to stop their blood pressure medication as soon as they feel better. What should you as a nurse do?

options.A: Agree that stopping is fine since the symptoms have temporarily disappeared
options.B: Suggest they sell the remaining pills to a neighbor with similar symptoms
options.C: Explain that chronic conditions require ongoing treatment and counsel them on adherence
options.D: Tell them to double the dose tomorrow to finish the medication faster

explanation: Brilliant nursing judgment! Chronic illnesses need continuous management, and patient education is our superpower as nurses. [learn more](GNS215_U1_T3#GNS215_U1_T3_h8)

question: How can frontline nurses directly help prevent medicine wastage in health clinics?

options.A: By refusing to treat patients who cannot pay cash upfront
options.B: By maintaining accurate inventory records and monitoring expiration dates
options.C: By hiding extra drug supplies in private lockers for emergencies
options.D: By ordering random medications without checking clinic records

explanation: You got it! Keeping a close eye on stock and expiry dates ensures medicines are used properly before they spoil. [learn more](GNS215_U1_T3#GNS215_U1_T3_h8)

question: What is the main feature of a unit dispensing system?

options.A: Medications are supplied in ready-to-administer individual doses
options.B: Nurses store large bulk supplies of drugs directly on the ward
options.C: Doctors dispense medications straight from the clinic consultation room
options.D: Patients purchase all their prescribed drugs from outside pharmacies

explanation: The core design of this system is to package drugs individually so they are ready for a specific patient at a specific time. [learn more](GNS215_U1_T4#GNS215_U1_T4_h1)

question: How does the unit dose system differ from traditional ward stock methods?

options.A: Nurses take over full responsibility for compounding intravenous fluids
options.B: Preparation shifts from busy clinical wards to the central pharmacy
options.C: Patients completely manage their own drug schedules without supervision
options.D: Hospital pharmacists no longer verify doctor prescriptions before supply

explanation: Moving the drug preparation task away from the noisy ward into the pharmacy reduces interruptions and lowers the risk of mistakes. [learn more](GNS215_U1_T4#GNS215_U1_T4_h1)

question: What was a major issue with patients bringing bulk drug supplies to Nigerian hospital wards?

options.A: Too many digital prescription logs
options.B: Poor storage conditions and lost medications
options.C: Excessive involvement of clinical pharmacists
options.D: Immediate electronic tracking of every pill

explanation: Bulk drugs kept in ward lockers were frequently misplaced, stolen, or exposed to heat and moisture, which ruined their potency. [learn more](GNS215_U1_T4#GNS215_U1_T4_h2)

question: How does unit dispensing improve financial transparency for patients?

options.A: Medication prices are standardized across all states
options.B: Hospital care becomes completely free of charge
options.C: Invoices are calculated based on hospital stay duration
options.D: Patients pay only for the exact doses administered

explanation: Instead of buying an entire pack of fifty tablets when only five are needed, the patient only pays for those five doses. [learn more](GNS215_U1_T4#GNS215_U1_T4_h2)

question: What is the primary purpose of a unit dose cart on a hospital ward?

options.A: Serving as an emergency resuscitation trolley for cardiac arrest
options.B: Holding individual patient medication drawers for safe rounds
options.C: Transporting large bulk fluid bags from the main central store
options.D: Storing personal medical files and patient charts securely

explanation: The unit dose cart contains separate locked or labeled sections for each patient so the nurse can administer drugs safely bed-to-bed. [learn more](GNS215_U1_T4#GNS215_U1_T4_h3)

question: Why is the patient medication profile essential in a unit dose setup?

options.A: It ensures that hospital billing departments track patient food preferences
options.B: It allows nurses to diagnose minor illnesses without consulting doctors
options.C: It replaces the need for any verbal or written communication on the ward
options.D: It gives pharmacists a clear, real-time record to check before supplying doses

explanation: The pharmacist relies on this active profile to verify dosages and catch potential drug interactions before packaging the individual doses. [learn more](GNS215_U1_T4#GNS215_U1_T4_h3)

question: What step immediately follows the physician writing a prescription in the unit dispensing workflow?

options.A: The pharmacist reviews and verifies the order
options.B: The ward cleaner organizes the medication cart
options.C: The nurse administers the drug immediately
options.D: The patient pays the hospital cashier

explanation: Before any medication is picked or packaged, the pharmacist must check the prescription for safety and correct dosing. [learn more](GNS215_U1_T4#GNS215_U1_T4_h4)

question: A nurse is preparing to give a 10:00 AM medication dose using the unit dispensing cart. When is the best time to document that the drug was given?

options.A: Whenever the nurse remembers during the afternoon visiting hours
options.B: Before leaving the central pharmacy room with the mobile drug cart
options.C: Immediately after the patient swallows the medication at the bedside
options.D: At the end of the shift when all patient charts are gathered together

explanation: Documentation must happen right after administration to prevent accidental double-dosing or missed records. [learn more](GNS215_U1_T4#GNS215_U1_T4_h4)

question: What is the main responsibility of the nurse at the bedside during unit dispensing?

options.A: Checking the chemical purity of drugs inside the pharmacy lab
options.B: Packaging the individual pills into small plastic wrappers
options.C: Performing final safety checks and administering the drug
options.D: Calculating the bulk wholesale cost of each medication dose

explanation: The nurse is the last person to see the patient before ingestion, making bedside verification essential to catch any lingering errors. [learn more](GNS215_U1_T4#GNS215_U1_T4_h5)

question: Which professional group acts as the primary defense against prescribing and dosage errors before drugs reach the ward?

options.A: Medical records clerks
options.B: Ward porters
options.C: Pharmacists
options.D: Hospital accountants

explanation: Pharmacists review the initial orders and verify clinical safety before preparing the individual doses for distribution. [learn more](GNS215_U1_T4#GNS215_U1_T4_h5)

question: Why does the unit dose system lead to fewer medication errors on the wards?

options.A: Nurses no longer need to check patient wristbands before giving drugs
options.B: Clear labeling and professional pharmacy preparation reduce guesswork
options.C: Doctors stop changing medication orders once the patient is admitted
options.D: Patients completely take over the responsibility of drug management

explanation: Pre-packaged, individually labeled doses remove the need for nurses to measure or split pills under high-pressure ward conditions. [learn more](GNS215_U1_T4#GNS215_U1_T4_h6)

question: How does unit dispensing help reduce financial waste in hospitals?

options.A: By tracking consumption accurately and allowing return of unsealed doses
options.B: By forcing patients to buy their medications from private vendors outside
options.C: By charging patients high penalty fees for missed medication doses
options.D: By eliminating the need for any professional pharmacy staff on duty

explanation: Precise tracking prevents excess purchasing, and sealed returned medications can be safely reissued to other patients. [learn more](GNS215_U1_T4#GNS215_U1_T4_h6)

question: What is a major manpower challenge when setting up unit dispensing in resource-limited hospitals?

options.A: Excessive numbers of idle staff wandering around the wards
options.B: Shortage of registered pharmacists and trained technicians
options.C: Too many foreign consultants interfering with local protocols
options.D: Unwillingness of nursing staff to work morning shifts

explanation: A lack of adequate professional staff creates bottlenecks in reviewing prescriptions and preparing individual doses on time. [learn more](GNS215_U1_T4#GNS215_U1_T4_h7)

question: Why do hospitals in resource-limited settings often start unit dispensing in high-risk units first?

options.A: To maximize safety impact where vulnerable patients need it most
options.B: To comply with international rules regarding surgical theatres only
options.C: To hide implementation failures from hospital management boards
options.D: To test equipment durability without involving any professional staff

explanation: Starting in units like intensive care or pediatrics targets areas where medication mistakes can cause the most severe harm. [learn more](GNS215_U1_T4#GNS215_U1_T4_h7)

question: What is a key policy step needed to improve medication dispensing systems nationally?

options.A: Making all prescription drugs completely free for every citizen
options.B: Transferring all nursing duties to the central pharmacy department
options.C: Banning the use of mobile carts in all public healthcare facilities
options.D: Including unit dose standards in hospital accreditation requirements

explanation: Enforcing standards through official accreditation ensures hospitals allocate necessary resources to maintain safe dispensing practices. [learn more](GNS215_U1_T4#GNS215_U1_T4_h8)

question: Which technology helps link patient prescriptions directly with pharmacy dispensing software?

options.A: Manual paper ledgers stored in wooden cabinets
options.B: Electronic health records and barcoding systems
options.C: Standard telephone landlines on the ward
options.D: Traditional wall clocks placed in the hallway

explanation: Digital records and barcode scanners speed up order transmission and reduce transcription mistakes between departments. [learn more](GNS215_U1_T4#GNS215_U1_T4_h8)

question: What is the main use of the Nigerian National Formulary?

options.A: To grade medical students on their pharmacology exam scores
options.B: To record the personal contact details of all licensed doctors
options.C: To provide a list of approved and safe medicines for healthcare use
options.D: To set the retail prices for all retail pharmacies in the country

explanation: Think of the formulary as your official handbook! It lists safe, approved medications you can trust when caring for patients in Nigerian hospitals. [learn more](GNS215_U1_T5#GNS215_U1_T5_h1)

question: Why is the formulary tied closely to the National Essential Medicines List?

options.A: It replaces the need for nurses to study pharmacology in school
options.B: It ensures hospitals stock medicines needed for the most common illnesses
options.C: It forces pharmaceutical companies to stop importing foreign products
options.D: It guarantees that every citizen receives free treatment at clinics

explanation: Spot on! Linking them makes sure hospitals focus on stocking the drugs our patients need most, like treatments for malaria and common infections. [learn more](GNS215_U1_T5#GNS215_U1_T5_h1)

question: Which agency is responsible for regulating food and drugs in Nigeria?

options.A: NAFDAC
options.B: Standard Organisation of Nigeria
options.C: National Youth Service Corps
options.D: Federal Ministry of Education

explanation: You've got this! NAFDAC is our watchdog, keeping watch over how drugs are made, imported, and sold across Nigeria. [learn more](GNS215_U1_T5#GNS215_U1_T5_h2)

question: How does following the Nigerian National Formulary help protect you as a nurse?

options.A: It allows them to prescribe any foreign drug without a doctor's order
options.B: It grants them the legal authority to open private retail pharmacies
options.C: It safeguards them from liability by using officially approved treatments
options.D: It exempts them from paying professional licensing renewal fees

explanation: Following approved national guidelines keeps you safe professionally. It shows you practiced according to standard, trusted nursing care! [learn more](GNS215_U1_T5#GNS215_U1_T5_h2)

question: What is looked at first when choosing drugs for the Nigerian Essential Medicines List?

options.A: How colorful the packaging of the drug is
options.B: The distance of the manufacturing country
options.C: Whether the drug has a pleasant sweet taste
options.D: Prevalence of the disease the drug treats

explanation: It's all about need! We prioritize drugs for the illnesses affecting the highest number of people in our communities. [learn more](GNS215_U1_T5#GNS215_U1_T5_h3)

question: Why must drugs chosen for the formulary stay stable in tropical climates?

options.A: To make the drug containers look attractive on hospital shelves
options.B: To ensure the tablets dissolve instantly when dropped in cold water
options.C: To prevent the medicine from degrading rapidly under local weather conditions
options.D: to guarantee the medication smells pleasant during administration

explanation: Nigeria's warm weather can break down chemicals quickly. Drugs must be tough enough to hold their strength in our local climate! [learn more](GNS215_U1_T5#GNS215_U1_T5_h3)

question: A patient with a mild viral cold is given three different strong antibiotics. What does this show?

options.A: The ideal use of the National Essential Medicines List
options.B: Irrational prescribing and potential misuse of drugs
options.C: An excellent example of standard clinical protocol
options.D: A necessary step to prevent common tropical diseases

explanation: Antibiotics don't cure viruses! Giving them unnecessarily is a classic example of drug misuse that we want to avoid. [learn more](GNS215_U1_T5#GNS215_U1_T5_h4)

question: What is a major danger of misusing drugs in healthcare settings?

options.A: Immediate reduction in the overall cost of running hospitals
options.B: Development of antimicrobial resistance to common infections
options.C: Faster recovery times for patients with chronic illnesses
options.D: Decreased workload for nurses on the hospital wards

explanation: When we overuse antibiotics, germs learn how to fight back and survive, making common infections much harder to treat later. [learn more](GNS215_U1_T5#GNS215_U1_T5_h4)

question: How are drugs mainly grouped inside the National Formulary?

options.A: By the alphabetical order of brand names
options.B: By pharmacological class and body systems
options.C: By the retail price in local open markets
options.D: By the country where the drug was imported

explanation: Grouping by body systems (like cardiovascular or respiratory) makes it super easy to find what you need during busy ward shifts. [learn more](GNS215_U1_T5#GNS215_U1_T5_h5)

question: Why is it best to look up medications by their generic name in the formulary?

options.A: It prevents confusion because one drug can have many different brand names
options.B: It stops patients from experiencing any side effects
options.C: It ensures the medication is always available free of charge
options.D: It proves that the drug was manufactured locally in Nigeria

explanation: A single drug can have dozens of brand names, but the generic name is always the same everywhere in the world! [learn more](GNS215_U1_T5#GNS215_U1_T5_h5)

question: Why should a nurse check the formulary before giving a drug to a patient?

options.A: To find out which commercial brand name is the most expensive
options.B: To calculate the daily profit margin of the hospital pharmacy department
options.C: To verify normal dosage ranges and check for potential adverse reactions
options.D: To order new stock supplies directly from foreign manufacturers

explanation: Checking first is a great habit! It helps you confirm the safe dose and watch out for side effects before administration. [learn more](GNS215_U1_T5#GNS215_U1_T5_h6)

question: You are about to give a patient a drug with a dosage you aren't sure about. What should you do?

options.A: Check the formulary or drug guide to confirm the correct safe dosage range
options.B: Administer the medication immediately to avoid delaying ward routines
options.C: Throw the medication away in the clinical waste bin without telling anyone
options.D: Ask another patient in the same ward what dose they usually take

explanation: Always double-check! Consulting a trusted drug guide keeps your patient safe and builds your clinical confidence. [learn more](GNS215_U1_T5#GNS215_U1_T5_h6)

question: What is the main goal of the Essential Drug Programme in public health?

options.A: Ensuring safe and affordable medicines are always available
options.B: Eliminating the need for doctors in rural clinics
options.C: Reducing the overall salaries of hospital pharmacy staff
options.D: Promoting only foreign-manufactured pharmaceutical brands

explanation: You got this! The whole point of the Essential Drug Programme is to make sure vital, quality medicines remain easy to get and affordable for everyone. [learn more](GNS215_U1_T6#GNS215_U1_T6_h1)

question: Why do nurses play such a big role in carrying out the Essential Drug Programme?

options.A: They work exclusively inside administrative pharmacy offices
options.B: They control the international import budgets for pharmaceuticals
options.C: They interact with patients daily and manage bedside drug use
options.D: They are legally licensed to manufacture commercial vaccines

explanation: Spot on! As a nurse, you are right on the frontline—giving medications, tracking supplies, and teaching patients every single day. [learn more](GNS215_U1_T6#GNS215_U1_T6_h1)

question: What official list guides healthcare workers on which medicines are approved for public health facilities?

options.A: Essential Medicines List
options.B: Standard Nursing Care Plan
options.C: Global Import Tariff Book
options.D: Private Pharmacy Catalog

explanation: Well done! The Essential Medicines List (EML) contains the carefully selected drugs needed to meet the priority healthcare needs of the community. [learn more](GNS215_U1_T6#GNS215_U1_T6_h2)

question: Why do clinics keep a 'buffer stock' of essential drugs?

options.A: To fulfill mandatory export quotas for foreign hospitals
options.B: To hide expired medications away from visiting inspectors
options.C: To prevent running out of drugs during unexpected supply delays
options.D: To increase the financial cost of routine patient treatments

explanation: Exactly! Think of buffer stock as your safety net so the clinic never runs dry when shipments are delayed. [learn more](GNS215_U1_T6#GNS215_U1_T6_h2)

question: Which inventory rule ensures that medicines closer to their expiration date are used first?

options.A: Most-Expensive, First-Used
options.B: First-Expired, First-Out
options.C: Random-Selection Method
options.D: First-In, Last-Out

explanation: Correct! FEFO (First-Expired, First-Out) helps prevent waste and patient risk by making sure older stock gets used before new deliveries. [learn more](GNS215_U1_T6#GNS215_U1_T6_h3)

question: You notice some insulin vials have been sitting on a warm desk for hours. What should you do?

options.A: Dilute the warm insulin with sterile water to restore its cold temperature
options.B: Consult the pharmacy or discard the compromised vials according to policy
options.C: Return them immediately to the patient refrigerator without checking
options.D: Administer them quickly before the expiration date arrives next month

explanation: You nailed it. Insulin is sensitive to heat and loses its potency when left out. Always check with pharmacy or follow safety rules rather than risking a patient's dose. [learn more](GNS215_U1_T6#GNS215_U1_T6_h3)

question: What is the term for giving a patient too many different medications than they actually need?

options.A: Polypharmacy
options.B: Placebo therapy
options.C: Prophylaxis
options.D: Pharmacovigilance

explanation: Good job! Polypharmacy means 'many drugs' and happens when patients take multiple medications at once, increasing the risk of side effects. [learn more](GNS215_U1_T6#GNS215_U1_T6_h4)

question: Why is rational drug use so important in the fight against antibiotic resistance?

options.A: It ensures that pharmaceutical companies make higher profits annually
options.B: It guarantees that all drugs are manufactured using local herbs only
options.C: It stops patients from ever visiting a public health facility again
options.D: It prevents the overuse and misuse of antibiotics that cause bacteria to mutate

explanation: Spot on! Using antibiotics wisely stops germs from learning how to beat our drugs. [learn more](GNS215_U1_T6#GNS215_U1_T6_h4)

question: What is the main goal of supporting a patient with their medication routine for a chronic illness?

options.A: Reducing the workload of the hospital records department
options.B: Forcing the patient to purchase expensive imported vitamins
options.C: Preventing the patient from asking questions about their care
options.D: Helping the patient take medications correctly and consistently

explanation: Correct! Adherence support is all about encouraging and helping patients stick to their treatment plan so they can get better. [learn more](GNS215_U1_T6#GNS215_U1_T6_h5)

question: A patient with a bacterial infection wants to stop taking antibiotics after two days because they feel fine. What should you tell them?

options.A: They must double the remaining dose on the third day instead
options.B: They should save the remaining pills for a headache next week
options.C: Stopping early can cause the infection to return stronger and more resistant
options.D: It is completely safe to stop once fever symptoms disappear

explanation: You got it! Always encourage patients to finish the full dose so the infection doesn't bounce back stronger. [learn more](GNS215_U1_T6#GNS215_U1_T6_h5)

question: What is the main focus of 'pharmacovigilance'?

options.A: Transporting bulk cargo across regional borders
options.B: Monitoring and reporting adverse drug reactions
options.C: Setting international market prices for herbal supplements
options.D: Manufacturing sterile equipment for surgical theatres

explanation: Well done! Pharmacovigilance is just a fancy word for watching out for and reporting drug side effects to keep patients safe. [learn more](GNS215_U1_T6#GNS215_U1_T6_h6)

question: Why are nurse reports on side effects so crucial even after a drug has been approved for sale?

options.A: Drug manufacturers refuse to test their products before public release
options.B: Clinical trials cannot uncover every rare reaction before a drug is sold
options.C: Pharmacists do not notice any patient reactions inside the dispensary
options.D: Hospitals are legally required to fine patients who experience side effects

explanation: Exactly! Pre-market tests are limited, so frontline nurses are vital for catching rare side effects once real people start taking the medication. [learn more](GNS215_U1_T6#GNS215_U1_T6_h6)

question: Who among the following is NOT typically part of the healthcare team managing essential drugs?

options.A: Medical doctor
options.B: Clinical pharmacist
options.C: International airline pilot
options.D: Registered nurse

explanation: Easy one! Pilots fly planes, while doctors, nurses, and pharmacists work together to manage patient medications. [learn more](GNS215_U1_T6#GNS215_U1_T6_h7)

question: How does teamwork between nurses, doctors, and pharmacists improve the Essential Drug Programme?

options.A: By removing the need for any internal hospital quality audits
options.B: By allowing nurses to take over surgical operations from physicians
options.C: By shifting all financial responsibilities entirely onto patients
options.D: By combining different professional skills to prevent drug errors and waste

explanation: Spot on! When healthcare professionals team up, they catch mistakes early and keep patients safe. [learn more](GNS215_U1_T6#GNS215_U1_T6_h7)

question: What does drug over-prescription mean in clinical practice?

options.A: Storing too many pharmaceutical products in the hospital pharmacy
options.B: Giving medicines that are unnecessary or in too high a dose
options.C: Ordering only herbal remedies instead of orthodox drugs
options.D: Failing to give any medication to a critically ill patient

explanation: Over-prescription happens when patients receive drugs they do not need or take excessive quantities that can harm them. [learn more](GNS215_U1_T7#GNS215_U1_T7_h1)

question: What is the main purpose of the National Drug Policy in Nigeria?

options.A: To ensure medicines are safe, effective, and properly used
options.B: To give nurses the sole legal power to write prescriptions
options.C: To make every single medication free for all citizens
options.D: To stop all foreign pharmaceutical companies from importing drugs

explanation: The policy sets standards to protect the public by regulating drug quality, distribution, and rational use. [learn more](GNS215_U1_T7#GNS215_U1_T7_h1)

question: Why do some patients pressure doctors to write unnecessary prescriptions?

options.A: They believe getting a drug means they received good care
options.B: They are legally required to buy three drugs per visit
options.C: They prefer paying more money for hospital visits
options.D: They want to study pharmacology at the university

explanation: Many patients feel unsatisfied with a consultation unless they walk away with physical items like tablets or syrups. [learn more](GNS215_U1_T7#GNS215_U1_T7_h2)

question: How can time pressure in a busy clinic contribute to over-prescription?

options.A: Doctors have more time to carefully review every single medical chart
options.B: Clinicians may quickly write prescriptions to end consultations faster
options.C: Nurses take over all prescribing duties to reduce doctor workload
options.D: Patients automatically leave the clinic without asking for drugs

explanation: When clinics are overcrowded, writing a prescription takes less time than explaining why a drug is not needed. [learn more](GNS215_U1_T7#GNS215_U1_T7_h2)

question: What is polypharmacy generally defined as?

options.A: Stopping all medications abruptly without advice
options.B: Taking five or more medications concurrently
options.C: Injecting a single drug twice a day
options.D: Using only traditional herbs for chronic illnesses

explanation: Polypharmacy refers to the use of multiple drugs at the same time, commonly set at a threshold of five or more. [learn more](GNS215_U1_T7#GNS215_U1_T7_h3)

question: What happens during a prescribing cascade?

options.A: The pharmacy runs out of basic supplies and substitutes vitamins
options.B: A drug side effect is mistaken for a new illness and treated with another drug
options.C: All medications are washed out of the patient's system at once
options.D: A nurse stops all prescriptions due to a sudden power outage

explanation: The prescribing cascade creates a dangerous cycle where side effects lead to more prescriptions instead of drug discontinuation. [learn more](GNS215_U1_T7#GNS215_U1_T7_h3)

question: What major public health threat is directly worsened by the over-prescription of antibiotics?

options.A: High blood pressure rates
options.B: Chronic kidney stone disease
options.C: Antimicrobial resistance
options.D: Nutritional vitamin deficiencies

explanation: Unnecessary antibiotic use teaches bacteria how to survive drug treatments, creating resistant strains that are hard to cure. [learn more](GNS215_U1_T7#GNS215_U1_T7_h4)

question: An elderly patient taking many unnecessary drugs is most at risk for which problem?

options.A: Rapid increase in daily physical activity
options.B: Sudden improvement in physical endurance
options.C: Severe adverse drug reactions and toxicity
options.D: Complete immunity to all common infections

explanation: Older adults process drugs more slowly, making them highly vulnerable to side effects and dangerous drug interactions. [learn more](GNS215_U1_T7#GNS215_U1_T7_h4)

question: What is a key action during a nursing medication review?

options.A: Telling the patient to stop taking all prescribed treatments
options.B: Changing the hospital's drug supply company without approval
options.C: Comparing prescribed drugs against the patient's current diagnoses
options.D: Ordering new laboratory equipment from foreign manufacturers

explanation: A proper review ensures every medication matches a genuine, active medical need rather than an outdated or unverified condition. [learn more](GNS215_U1_T7#GNS215_U1_T7_h5)

question: Why is it important to ask patients about herbal supplements during a medication review?

options.A: To calculate the exact financial cost of traditional medicines
options.B: To replace all hospital pharmacies with local herb shops
options.C: To report illegal herbal sellers to the local police department
options.D: To check for hidden interactions with prescribed orthodox drugs

explanation: Herbal products can interact strongly with prescription medications, altering their effects or increasing toxicity. [learn more](GNS215_U1_T7#GNS215_U1_T7_h5)

question: What is one effective nursing action during a multidisciplinary ward round?

options.A: Writing new drug orders without consulting the attending doctor
options.B: Hiding the prescription chart from the medical team
options.C: Discharging all patients who take more than two tablets daily
options.D: Questioning unnecessary prescriptions and suggesting alternatives

explanation: Nurses act as safety advocates by speaking up when a medication order appears unsafe or clinically unjustified. [learn more](GNS215_U1_T7#GNS215_U1_T7_h6)

question: How does educating a patient help reduce inappropriate drug use?

options.A: It prevents them from ever visiting a hospital clinic again
options.B: It helps them understand why they do not need certain medicines
options.C: It forces pharmaceutical companies to lower medication prices
options.D: It gives them the legal right to prescribe drugs to neighbors

explanation: When patients understand the risks of unnecessary drugs, they are less likely to demand them from clinicians. [learn more](GNS215_U1_T7#GNS215_U1_T7_h6)

question: Which Nigerian agency is heavily involved in regulating drug safety and distribution?

options.A: Nigerian Meteorological Agency
options.B: National Youth Service Corps
options.C: NAFDAC
options.D: Federal Road Safety Corps

explanation: NAFDAC is the primary federal agency responsible for regulating and controlling the manufacture, importation, and sale of drugs in Nigeria. [learn more](GNS215_U1_T7#GNS215_U1_T7_h7)

question: What is the main goal of hospital antibiotic stewardship programs?

options.A: To encourage patients to take antibiotics for common colds
options.B: To ban all antibiotics from being stored in the country
options.C: To make expensive antibiotics available for free to staff
options.D: To promote the correct, rational use of antimicrobial drugs

explanation: Stewardship programs monitor and guide prescribing practices to prevent misuse and slow down antimicrobial resistance. [learn more](GNS215_U1_T7#GNS215_U1_T7_h7)

question: Why is drug under-prescription often a hidden problem in healthcare?

options.A: Pharmacies automatically correct the missing prescriptions
options.B: It is completely illegal and hidden by hospital administrators
options.C: Patients refuse to report when their doctor forgets a drug
options.D: It involves omissions of care rather than active errors that cause immediate toxicity

explanation: Great job thinking about patient safety! When something is left out (an omission), it doesn't cause a sudden toxic reaction, making it much harder to spot right away compared to an overdose. [learn more](GNS215_U1_T8#GNS215_U1_T8_h1)

question: Which group of patients is most often affected by drug under-prescription?

options.A: Children admitted for acute infectious diseases
options.B: Young healthy adults visiting emergency rooms
options.C: Athletes recovering from orthopedic surgeries
options.D: Older adults and those with multiple chronic illnesses

explanation: Spot on! Older patients and those with complex health issues often miss out on necessary care because healthcare providers worry too much about drug interactions. [learn more](GNS215_U1_T8#GNS215_U1_T8_h2)

question: A patient with mild kidney disease is denied a standard heart medication because the doctor worries about organ damage. What does this show?

options.A: Forgetting to check the patient's medical history chart
options.B: Failing to prescribe due to high pharmacy costs
options.C: Deliberately stopping all medications during palliative care
options.D: Withholding therapy out of fear rather than adjusting the dose

explanation: You've got this! Instead of finding a safe dose adjusted for the kidneys, the doctor avoided the drug entirely out of fear. [learn more](GNS215_U1_T8#GNS215_U1_T8_h2)

question: What is 'clinical inertia' when it comes to prescribing medications?

options.A: The rapid changing of medications by multiple different doctors
options.B: The failure of a provider to start or increase therapy when needed
options.C: The delay in pharmacy delivery of critical care drugs
options.D: The complete refusal of a patient to take prescribed pills

explanation: Clinical inertia is just a fancy way of saying healthcare providers sticking to the status quo instead of updating a treatment plan when a patient needs more help. [learn more](GNS215_U1_T8#GNS215_U1_T8_h3)

question: How can a fear of side effects lead to drug under-prescription?

options.A: Doctors prescribe double doses to prevent side effects
options.B: Providers choose to omit necessary treatments to avoid potential harm
options.C: Patients stop buying drugs that cause mild stomach upset
options.D: Pharmacists refuse to fill prescriptions for elderly patients

explanation: Exactly! Sometimes being overly scared of side effects stops a practitioner from starting a drug that could actually do the patient a lot of good. [learn more](GNS215_U1_T8#GNS215_U1_T8_h3)

question: What is the main purpose of medication reconciliation in clinical practice?

options.A: To report pharmaceutical companies for high drug prices
options.B: To compare current medication orders against what the patient actually needs
options.C: To destroy expired medications found in the patient bedside locker
options.D: To calculate the total monthly cost of all prescribed drugs

explanation: Medication reconciliation is like a safety net! It helps catch missing medications that should be part of the patient's treatment plan. [learn more](GNS215_U1_T8#GNS215_U1_T8_h4)

question: When is medication reconciliation most important for catching under-prescriptions?

options.A: At every transition of care, such as hospital admission or discharge
options.B: Right before a nurse administers a single daily dose
options.C: Only when a patient complains of severe allergic reactions
options.D: During routine annual physical exams in an outpatient clinic

explanation: Spot on! Transitions (like moving from the ward home or to another unit) are high-risk times when necessary medications easily get left behind or forgotten. [learn more](GNS215_U1_T8#GNS215_U1_T8_h4)

question: What is a common result of drug under-prescription?

options.A: Silent disease progression and preventable complications
options.B: Acute drug overdose and immediate hospital admission
options.C: Severe allergic reactions across multiple organ systems
options.D: Rapid development of antibiotic resistance in the community

explanation: You're building great clinical intuition! Under-prescription often harms patients quietly because their illness isn't being treated aggressively enough, leading to preventable setbacks. [learn more](GNS215_U1_T8#GNS215_U1_T8_h5)

question: A patient with a history of heart attacks is discharged without being given a statin or beta-blocker. What is this patient at higher risk for?

options.A: Immediate kidney failure caused by excessive medication
options.B: Acute drug toxicity from an accidental double dose
options.C: Severe antibiotic resistance from prolonged drug exposure
options.D: A recurrent cardiac event due to lack of secondary prevention

explanation: Brilliant! Leaving out essential recovery drugs (secondary prevention) significantly increases the chance that the patient might suffer another heart attack or stroke. [learn more](GNS215_U1_T8#GNS215_U1_T8_h5)

question: How can nurses directly help reduce the problem of under-prescription?

options.A: By replacing missing physician orders with over-the-counter remedies
options.B: By advocating for evidence-based treatments during multidisciplinary rounds
options.C: By writing independent prescriptions for specialized cardiac drugs
options.D: By discharging patients early when medications are unavailable

explanation: You got it! Because nurses spend the most time with patients, they are in the best position to spot missing therapies and speak up during team meetings. [learn more](GNS215_U1_T8#GNS215_U1_T8_h6)

question: Why is patient education a powerful nursing tool against under-prescription?

options.A: It ensures patients refuse all medications to save money
options.B: It empowers patients to ask their doctors about standard therapies for their illness
options.C: It prevents doctors from making any clinical errors during visits
options.D: It teaches patients how to fill their own prescriptions at the pharmacy

explanation: Knowledge is power! When patients understand what treatments are standard for their condition, they can speak up and ask if their care plan includes them. [learn more](GNS215_U1_T8#GNS215_U1_T8_h6)

question: How many daily medications do doctors usually mean when they talk about polypharmacy?

options.A: Taking two or more medications daily
options.B: Taking ten or more medications daily
options.C: Taking only herbal remedies alongside drugs
options.D: Taking five or more medications daily

explanation: You'll often hear this in the ward! Polypharmacy simply means a patient is taking five or more regular medications at the same time. [learn more](GNS215_U1_T9#GNS215_U1_T9_h1)

question: What is the main difference between good (appropriate) polypharmacy and bad (problematic) polypharmacy?

options.A: Problematic polypharmacy only occurs in hospital intensive care units.
options.B: Problematic polypharmacy means the patient refuses to swallow pills.
options.C: Appropriate polypharmacy has clear clinical benefits that outweigh risks.
options.D: Appropriate polypharmacy involves only traditional herbal mixtures.
