question: Which of the following is NOT a standard nursing duty during a poisoning emergency?

options.A: Collecting and labeling biological samples for analysis
options.B: Synthesizing new chemical antidotes in the hospital pharmacy
options.C: Ensuring personal protective equipment is worn correctly
options.D: Monitoring vital signs and watching for sudden clinical changes

explanation: Nurses monitor patients, use safety gear, and collect labs, but we leave the chemical manufacturing to the pharmacists! [learn more](GNS215_U5_T1#GNS215_U5_T1_h6)

question: What is the primary role of the nurse regarding drug hazards?

options.A: Serving as the final safety barrier before administration
options.B: Manufacturing safer pharmaceutical compounds for hospital use
options.C: Determining the exact chemical composition of all prescribed drugs
options.D: Prescribing alternative medications to avoid dangerous side effects

explanation: Nurses check medications right before giving them to catch errors made earlier in the process. [learn more](GNS215_U5_T2#GNS215_U5_T2_h1)

question: Why must a nurse view pharmacotherapy as a balance between benefits and risks?

options.A: Therapeutic effects only occur when toxic reactions are actively triggered
options.B: Patients will refuse treatment if they know about any potential side effects
options.C: Every medication carries some level of inherent hazard alongside its healing properties
options.D: Hospital policies require reporting all minor medication side effects daily

explanation: All drugs have the potential to cause harm, so nurses must weigh therapeutic gains against possible toxic effects. [learn more](GNS215_U5_T2#GNS215_U5_T2_h1)

question: Which type of adverse drug reaction is predictable and related to the drug's normal pharmacological action?

options.A: Type B
options.B: Type D
options.C: Type A
options.D: Type C

explanation: Type A reactions are augmented pharmacological effects that happen because the drug is working too strongly. [learn more](GNS215_U5_T2#GNS215_U5_T2_h2)

question: A patient develops a sudden, severe allergic skin rash after taking a common antibiotic for the first time. How is this reaction classified?

options.A: Type A
options.B: Type E
options.C: Type B
options.D: Type C

explanation: Type B reactions are bizarre, unpredictable, and do not relate to the drug's normal pharmacological effects. [learn more](GNS215_U5_T2#GNS215_U5_T2_h2)

question: What is the main result of impaired drug excretion by the kidneys?

options.A: Rapid elimination of the drug through the skin
options.B: Drug accumulation and potential toxicity in the body
options.C: Immediate breakdown of the drug in the stomach
options.D: Increased therapeutic effectiveness with zero side effects

explanation: When kidneys cannot filter waste properly, drugs stay in the blood longer and build up to dangerous levels. [learn more](GNS215_U5_T2#GNS215_U5_T2_h3)

question: Why can a standard, correct dose of a medication still cause toxicity in certain individuals?

options.A: All standard doses are actually calculated to cause mild toxicity first
options.B: Slowed organ clearance can cause the drug to build up over time
options.C: Standard doses only work if the patient takes them with food
options.D: The liver automatically destroys standard doses before they work

explanation: If liver or kidney function is reduced, normal doses cannot be cleared fast enough, leading to toxic buildup. [learn more](GNS215_U5_T2#GNS215_U5_T2_h3)

question: Why are neonates especially vulnerable to drug toxicity?

options.A: Immature liver enzymes and undeveloped kidney filtration
options.B: An unusually high metabolic rate that burns up medications
options.C: A complete lack of blood circulation to internal organs
options.D: Increased total body fat that traps water-soluble drugs

explanation: Babies cannot break down and excrete drugs efficiently because their organs are still developing. [learn more](GNS215_U5_T2#GNS215_U5_T2_h4)

question: A patient with severe liver disease is prescribed a medication that is normally broken down by hepatic enzymes. What is the most appropriate nursing concern?

options.A: The liver disease will instantly cure itself once the pill is swallowed
options.B: The drug may build up in the body and cause toxic effects
options.C: The medication will pass through the body without any effect at all
options.D: The drug will be eliminated too quickly to provide any relief

explanation: A damaged liver cannot metabolize drugs effectively, leading to dangerous levels accumulating in the bloodstream. [learn more](GNS215_U5_T2#GNS215_U5_T2_h4)

question: What is the primary effect of grapefruit juice on certain medications?

options.A: Binding directly to the drug to prevent any absorption
options.B: Inhibiting intestinal enzymes and increasing drug blood levels
options.C: Speeding up kidney excretion to reduce drug effectiveness
options.D: Neutralizing the chemical pH of the drug in the stomach

explanation: Grapefruit juice blocks specific enzymes in the gut, allowing much more medication to enter the bloodstream. [learn more](GNS215_U5_T2#GNS215_U5_T2_h5)

question: What happens when a patient takes two different medications that both depress the central nervous system?

options.A: Liver enzymes shut down permanently to prevent any chemical processing
options.B: An additive or synergistic sedative effect that can impair breathing
options.C: The two drugs cancel each other out completely with no effect
options.D: The patient experiences a sudden burst of high physical energy

explanation: Combining multiple depressants multiplies their calming effects on the brain and can dangerously slow breathing. [learn more](GNS215_U5_T2#GNS215_U5_T2_h5)

question: Which action must a nurse take BEFORE giving a high-risk medication?

options.A: Ask the patient to sign a waiver releasing the hospital from liability
options.B: Gather baseline clinical data and relevant lab values
options.C: Discontinue all other medications the patient is currently taking
options.D: Double the prescribed dose to test for allergic reactions

explanation: Baseline checks give you a reference point to compare against if the patient develops adverse symptoms later. [learn more](GNS215_U5_T2#GNS215_U5_T2_h6)

question: A patient taking a new blood pressure medication suddenly feels very dizzy and lightheaded when standing up. What is the most appropriate immediate nursing action?

options.A: Tell the patient to run in place to improve blood circulation
options.B: Administer a stimulant medication to raise the blood pressure
options.C: Check the patient's blood pressure and pulse immediately
options.D: Wait until the next scheduled clinic visit to report the finding

explanation: Dizziness after starting a new blood pressure drug points to orthostatic hypotension, requiring a check of vital signs. [learn more](GNS215_U5_T2#GNS215_U5_T2_h6)

question: What is the very first action a nurse should take when a patient shows signs of severe drug toxicity?

options.A: Stop the administration of the offending medication
options.B: Increase the intravenous fluid rate without a doctor's order
options.C: Document the event in the patient's chart at the end of the shift
options.D: Ask the patient to walk around the room to stay awake

explanation: Stopping the drug source prevents any more of the toxic substance from entering the patient's system. [learn more](GNS215_U5_T2#GNS215_U5_T2_h7)

question: Why are intravenous fluids often ordered for a patient experiencing drug toxicity?

options.A: To instantly neutralize the chemical pH of all oral medications
options.B: To help flush water-soluble drugs out through the kidneys
options.C: To dilute the remaining blood cells in the circulatory system
options.D: To replace liver tissue damaged by the toxic substance

explanation: Hydration supports kidney output, helping the body eliminate circulating toxins faster through urine. [learn more](GNS215_U5_T2#GNS215_U5_T2_h7)

question: What is the main goal of pharmacovigilance in healthcare?

options.A: Marketing new pharmaceutical products to regional hospitals
options.B: Detecting, assessing, and preventing adverse drug effects
options.C: Speeding up the clinical drug trial approval process
options.D: Calculating the financial cost of manufactured medications

explanation: Pharmacovigilance is the ongoing safety monitoring process designed to catch and prevent drug-related harm. [learn more](GNS215_U5_T2#GNS215_U5_T2_h8)

question: Why is it important to report medication near-misses and errors through institutional incident reporting systems?

options.A: It helps the healthcare team identify systemic flaws to prevent future harm
options.B: It allows the pharmacy to bill the insurance company for wasted drugs
options.C: It ensures that negligent nurses are immediately fired from the facility
options.D: It provides legal protection for the hospital during malpractice lawsuits

explanation: Reporting errors highlights weak spots in the medication system so safety procedures can be improved. [learn more](GNS215_U5_T2#GNS215_U5_T2_h8)

question: What type of chemical agent causes visible destruction of living tissue upon contact?

options.A: Irritants
options.B: Carcinogens
options.C: Sensitizers
options.D: Corrosives

explanation: Corrosive chemicals include strong acids and bases that directly destroy biological tissues on contact. [learn more](GNS215_U5_T3#GNS215_U5_T3_h1)

question: A cleaning solvent enters the bloodstream and damages the kidneys. What type of toxin is this?

options.A: Surface corrosive
options.B: Local irritant
options.C: Systemic toxin
options.D: Skin sensitizer

explanation: Systemic toxins travel through the bloodstream to affect specific internal organ systems far from the initial entry site. [learn more](GNS215_U5_T3#GNS215_U5_T3_h1)

question: Which organ serves as the primary site for metabolizing absorbed chemical toxins in the human body?

options.A: Lungs
options.B: Kidneys
options.C: Liver
options.D: Stomach

explanation: The liver contains specialized enzymes that break down and biotransform foreign chemicals before excretion. [learn more](GNS215_U5_T3#GNS215_U5_T3_h2)

question: A nurse breathes in fumes from an open disinfectant container. What is the main route of exposure here?

options.A: Injection
options.B: Inhalation
options.C: Absorption
options.D: Ingestion

explanation: Breathing in airborne vapors or gases directly introduces chemical agents into the respiratory tract and lungs. [learn more](GNS215_U5_T3#GNS215_U5_T3_h2)

question: Cellular respiration stops when certain toxins block processes inside which part of the cell?

options.A: Golgi apparatus
options.B: Mitochondria
options.C: Ribosomes
options.D: Cell membrane

explanation: Mitochondria are the powerhouses of the cell where cellular respiration occurs, making them a primary target for metabolic poisons. [learn more](GNS215_U5_T3#GNS215_U5_T3_h3)

question: Why do some toxic chemical exposures not show immediate symptoms?

options.A: Toxic chemicals remain entirely dormant in the bloodstream without interacting with cells.
options.B: Some agents cause slow, low-level damage that takes years to show up clinically.
options.C: The human body completely neutralizes all toxic substances automatically over time.
options.D: Initial symptoms are always hidden by the immune system's inflammatory response.

explanation: Cumulative low-level exposure slowly damages tissue over a long period before disease symptoms become obvious. [learn more](GNS215_U5_T3#GNS215_U5_T3_h3)

question: What is a common lung problem caused by breathing in toxic chemical fumes?

options.A: Renal failure
options.B: Pulmonary edema
options.C: Skin blistering
options.D: Abdominal cramps

explanation: Inhaled chemical irritants damage lung tissue and lead to fluid accumulation within the alveoli. [learn more](GNS215_U5_T3#GNS215_U5_T3_h4)

question: A patient presents with sudden confusion, tremors, and dizziness after working with industrial solvents. What organ system is primarily affected?

options.A: Integumentary system
options.B: Gastrointestinal system
options.C: Musculoskeletal system
options.D: Nervous system

explanation: Solvents often cross the blood-brain barrier, causing acute neurological symptoms like dizziness and tremors. [learn more](GNS215_U5_T3#GNS215_U5_T3_h4)

question: Why should you avoid making a patient vomit after they swallow a strong corrosive chemical?

options.A: The chemical instantly solidifies inside the stomach lining.
options.B: It neutralizes the stomach acid and stops normal digestion.
options.C: Regurgitation causes second burns to the food pipe (esophagus).
options.D: Vomiting pushes the chemical deeper into the lower intestine.

explanation: Passing a corrosive chemical back up through the esophagus exposes delicate tissues to a second round of severe burning. [learn more](GNS215_U5_T3#GNS215_U5_T3_h5)

question: What is the first thing to do when a chemical splashes directly into a patient's eyes?

options.A: Waiting for laboratory confirmation tests
options.B: Continuous flushing with water or saline
options.C: Instilling strong neutralizing acid drops
options.D: Applying an airtight eye patch immediately

explanation: Immediate flushing dilutes and removes the chemical agent before it can permanently damage the corneal tissue. [learn more](GNS215_U5_T3#GNS215_U5_T3_h5)

question: What type of medicine is used to bind heavy metals so the body can get rid of them?

options.A: Chelating agents
options.B: Inhaled corticosteroids
options.C: Vasopressor amines
options.D: Broad-spectrum antibiotics

explanation: Chelating drugs bind tightly to heavy metal ions so the body can excrete them safely through the urine. [learn more](GNS215_U5_T3#GNS215_U5_T3_h6)

question: Why is atropine administered to a patient experiencing organophosphate poisoning?

options.A: It coats the stomach lining to prevent absorption.
options.B: It blocks excess acetylcholine at receptor sites.
options.C: It chelates the poison out of the bloodstream.
options.D: It destroys the chemical structure of the pesticide.

explanation: Organophosphates build up acetylcholine, and atropine blocks those receptors to stop life-threatening overstimulation. [learn more](GNS215_U5_T3#GNS215_U5_T3_h6)

question: Where can healthcare workers find detailed safety and emergency information for a specific chemical?

options.A: Patient admission chart
options.B: Nursing care textbook
options.C: Safety Data Sheet
options.D: Hospital billing ledger

explanation: Safety Data Sheets provide comprehensive technical data regarding chemical hazards, handling precautions, and emergency responses. [learn more](GNS215_U5_T3#GNS215_U5_T3_h7)

question: Which of the following is NOT a primary nursing responsibility regarding workplace chemical safety?

options.A: Using appropriate personal protective equipment during tasks
options.B: Adhering strictly to institutional chemical handling guidelines
options.C: Formulating federal safety legislation for chemical manufacturing plants
options.D: Ensuring secondary containers are properly and clearly labeled

explanation: Legislative policymaking is handled by government regulatory bodies, whereas clinical nurses focus on safe handling and workplace protocols. [learn more](GNS215_U5_T3#GNS215_U5_T3_h7)

question: What timeframe typically defines an immediate drug reaction after administration?

options.A: After several months of therapy
options.B: Between one to two weeks
options.C: Exactly twenty-four hours later
options.D: Within minutes to a few hours

explanation: Immediate reactions manifest rapidly after exposure, often within minutes to a few hours. [learn more](GNS215_U5_T4#GNS215_U5_T4_h1)

question: Why must nurses watch patients closely right after giving medications?

options.A: To ensure patients swallow pills without water
options.B: To document exact drug manufacturing lot numbers
options.C: To prevent sudden and life-threatening body collapse
options.D: To calculate daily fluid balance accurately

explanation: Immediate drug reactions can escalate quickly, requiring instant nursing intervention to prevent severe harm. [learn more](GNS215_U5_T4#GNS215_U5_T4_h1)

question: Which antibody is mainly responsible for Type I immediate allergic reactions?

options.A: Immunoglobulin G
options.B: Immunoglobulin E
options.C: Immunoglobulin M
options.D: Immunoglobulin A

explanation: Type I hypersensitivity reactions are driven by IgE antibodies bound to mast cells and basophils. [learn more](GNS215_U5_T4#GNS215_U5_T4_h2)

question: What happens in the body when histamine is released during an acute drug reaction?

options.A: Widespread narrowing of peripheral blood vessels
options.B: Blood vessels widen and leak fluid into tissues
options.C: Immediate stopping of smooth muscle activity
options.D: Total block of all inflammatory pathways

explanation: Histamine causes blood vessels to dilate and leak fluid into tissues, leading to swelling and low blood pressure. [learn more](GNS215_U5_T4#GNS215_U5_T4_h2)

question: A patient has only a mild rash and slight itching after taking a drug. How is this reaction classified?

options.A: Moderate reaction
options.B: Severe reaction
options.C: Anaphylactic shock
options.D: Mild reaction

explanation: Localized skin symptoms without systemic involvement are classified as mild drug reactions. [learn more](GNS215_U5_T4#GNS215_U5_T4_h3)

question: Which clinical sign turns a mild drug reaction into a severe emergency?

options.A: Itching only on the spot where the injection was given
options.B: Trouble breathing and dangerous drop in blood pressure
options.C: A mild rash appearing twenty-four hours later
options.D: Slight stomach upset with normal vital signs

explanation: Shock and compromised airways indicate severe systemic failure requiring emergency intervention. [learn more](GNS215_U5_T4#GNS215_U5_T4_h3)

question: What happens to a patient's blood pressure during severe anaphylactic shock?

options.A: It drops very low
options.B: It goes very high
options.C: It stays slow and steady
options.D: It remains completely normal

explanation: Widespread vasodilation causes a sharp drop in blood pressure during anaphylaxis. [learn more](GNS215_U5_T4#GNS215_U5_T4_h4)

question: A patient getting penicillin starts wheezing, has swollen lips, and feels dizzy. What is likely happening?

options.A: A normal side effect of antibiotics
options.B: A severe allergic reaction affecting the whole body
options.C: A delayed skin reaction to the drug
options.D: Irritation right at the needle insertion spot

explanation: Simultaneous respiratory, skin, and cardiovascular symptoms point directly to systemic anaphylaxis. [learn more](GNS215_U5_T4#GNS215_U5_T4_h4)

question: What is the very first thing a nurse should do if an acute drug reaction starts?

options.A: Stop the drug infusion immediately
options.B: Leave the bedside to call a doctor
options.C: Give an oral anti-allergy tablet
options.D: Write down what is happening in the patient's chart

explanation: Halting further administration of the causative agent stops ongoing systemic exposure. [learn more](GNS215_U5_T4#GNS215_U5_T4_h5)

question: Why should the nurse keep the intravenous line open with normal saline after stopping the trigger drug?

options.A: To measure urine output through a catheter
options.B: To have a ready line for emergency fluids and medications
options.C: To wash out the mouth before giving oxygen
options.D: To dilute any remaining medicine in the stomach

explanation: An open IV line allows rapid administration of emergency medications and intravenous fluids for blood pressure support. [learn more](GNS215_U5_T4#GNS215_U5_T4_h5)

question: How often should you check vital signs during an active, severe drug reaction?

options.A: Once every four hours as per routine
options.B: Once a day during morning handover
options.C: Only after the emergency drugs have finished working
options.D: Every few minutes until the patient is stable

explanation: Frequent interval tracking is essential to catch sudden hemodynamic shifts during acute reactions. [learn more](GNS215_U5_T4#GNS215_U5_T4_h6)

question: What does a fast heart rate and falling oxygen level mean during a drug reaction?

options.A: The heart and lungs are struggling
options.B: The patient is having a normal recovery
options.C: The patient is well hydrated and stable
options.D: The allergy medicine is working well

explanation: Tachycardia and desaturation reflect compensatory stress and failing respiratory function. [learn more](GNS215_U5_T4#GNS215_U5_T4_h6)

question: Which drug is given first to treat sudden, severe anaphylaxis?

options.A: Paracetamol
options.B: Hydrocortisone
options.C: Epinephrine
options.D: Promethazine

explanation: Epinephrine is the essential first-line drug that reverses airway constriction and vascular collapse. [learn more](GNS215_U5_T4#GNS215_U5_T4_h7)

question: Why is emergency epinephrine given into the thigh muscle instead of under the skin?

options.A: The thigh muscle has fewer nerve endings
options.B: Injections under the skin destroy muscle tissue
options.C: It is less painful for adults
options.D: It enters the bloodstream much faster from muscle

explanation: Intramuscular injection into the vastus lateralis ensures rapid systemic absorption during emergencies. [learn more](GNS215_U5_T4#GNS215_U5_T4_h7)

question: Which detail is NOT needed when writing an incident report for an acute drug reaction?

options.A: The exact time the symptoms started
options.B: The patient's home address and phone number
options.C: The exact name of the drug that caused the reaction
options.D: The emergency treatments given

explanation: Clinical documentation focuses on the incident specifics rather than demographic contact details. [learn more](GNS215_U5_T4#GNS215_U5_T4_h8)

question: Why do healthcare systems track and report adverse drug reactions?

options.A: To calculate hospital revenue and pharmacy stock
options.B: To punish nurses who make mistakes
options.C: To decide standard ward accommodation fees
options.D: To monitor drug safety trends across different hospitals

explanation: Pharmacovigilance reporting helps national bodies track adverse drug patterns and protect public health. [learn more](GNS215_U5_T4#GNS215_U5_T4_h8)

question: Why is inhaling a chemical often more dangerous than getting it on your skin?

options.A: Rapid absorption into the bloodstream through the lungs
options.B: Localized swelling of the eye tissues
options.C: Delayed stomach ulceration and internal bleeding
options.D: Immediate burning of the outer skin layers

explanation: Think of the lungs as a massive highway into the body! Inhaled substances quickly cross into the tiny blood vessels (capillaries) in the lungs and travel straight to vital organs. [learn more](GNS215_U5_T5#GNS215_U5_T5_h1)

question: Why is figuring out how a chemical entered the body so important for your nursing care?

options.A: It replaces the need for vital sign monitoring during triage
options.B: It confirms the exact chemical formula without laboratory testing
options.C: It determines the exact financial cost of the hospital stay
options.D: It guides immediate decontamination steps and predicts systemic risks

explanation: Knowing the entry route helps you act fast—like washing skin or flushing eyes—and lets you anticipate which body organs are in the greatest danger. [learn more](GNS215_U5_T5#GNS215_U5_T5_h1)

question: Which sign warns you that a patient's upper airway might soon close up after inhaling a chemical?

options.A: Hoarseness or a stridor breathing sound
options.B: High urine output during the first hour
options.C: A slow and steady heart rate of 60 beats per minute
options.D: Warm and dry skin across the chest and arms

explanation: When a patient's voice suddenly changes or you hear a high-pitched whistling sound (stridor) when they breathe, their upper airway is swelling up. Act fast! [learn more](GNS215_U5_T5#GNS215_U5_T5_h2)

question: A patient arrives struggling to breathe and has blue lips after inhaling toxic fumes. What is your very first nursing priority?

options.A: Ask family members what chemical was spilled
options.B: Draw blood samples for a complete blood count
options.C: Ensure a patent airway and provide high-flow oxygen
options.D: Document the exact time of the workplace accident

explanation: Always remember ABC! Saving a life by securing the airway and giving oxygen comes way before asking questions or running tests. [learn more](GNS215_U5_T5#GNS215_U5_T5_h2)

question: What kind of pupil change do you expect to see in a patient with organophosphate poisoning (cholinergic toxidrome)?

options.A: Pinpoint pupils
options.B: Unreactive fixed pupils
options.C: Widely dilated pupils
options.D: Unequal pupil sizes

explanation: Organophosphates overstimulate the nervous system, which famously causes the pupils to shrink down to tiny, pinpoint sizes (miosis). [learn more](GNS215_U5_T5#GNS215_U5_T5_h3)

question: Why is spotting a specific 'toxidrome' (group of symptoms) so helpful in emergency care?

options.A: It proves legal liability for workplace safety violations
options.B: It stops the chemical from absorbing through unbroken skin
options.C: It guides rapid clinical management before lab tests confirm the toxin
options.D: It eliminates the need to decontaminate the patient's clothing

explanation: Lab tests take time! Spotting a familiar pattern of symptoms lets you start life-saving antidotes and care right away. [learn more](GNS215_U5_T5#GNS215_U5_T5_h3)

question: What is your very first step when a patient has dry chemical powder spilled all over their skin?

options.A: Wrap the area tightly with a clean sterile bandage
options.B: Scrub the affected skin vigorously with a stiff brush
options.C: Apply a thick layer of petroleum jelly over the powder
options.D: Brush away the loose powder before using water

explanation: Always brush dry powder off first! Adding water right away to some chemicals can trigger a fiery reaction or make the chemical burn worse. [learn more](GNS215_U5_T5#GNS215_U5_T5_h4)

question: Why do alkaline chemical burns (like lye) often cause deeper tissue damage than acid burns?

options.A: Alkalis cool down the skin cells and stop normal blood circulation
options.B: Acidic chemicals evaporate instantly upon touching human skin
options.C: Acidic solutions cannot pass through the outer layer of fat cells
options.D: Alkalis cause liquefactive necrosis, letting them penetrate deeper into tissue

explanation: Alkalis trigger a process called liquefactive necrosis that dissolves proteins and fats, allowing the chemical to burrow deep into the body. [learn more](GNS215_U5_T5#GNS215_U5_T5_h4)

question: Which blood test result is a classic warning sign of severe internal poisoning from swallowed toxins?

options.A: An elevated platelet level
options.B: A high white blood cell count
options.C: A low serum sodium level
options.D: An increased anion gap

explanation: An increased anion gap tells you there is a buildup of hidden, dangerous acids circulating in the patient's blood. [learn more](GNS215_U5_T5#GNS215_U5_T5_h5)

question: A patient with completely clear breathing sounds inhaled a toxic gas two hours ago. What should you, as the nurse, expect to do?

options.A: Withholding all intravenous fluids to prevent lung fluid overload
options.B: Ordering a baseline chest X-ray and monitoring for delayed edema
options.C: Performing an immediate surgical tracheostomy in the ward
options.D: Discharging the patient immediately since lungs are currently clear

explanation: Don't let clear lungs fool you! Inhaled toxins can trigger dangerous fluid buildup (edema) in the lungs hours later, so keep a close eye on them. [learn more](GNS215_U5_T5#GNS215_U5_T5_h5)

question: Which chemical exposure patient needs to be rushed straight to the resuscitation bay?

options.A: A patient with normal vital signs and no symptoms
options.B: A patient with abnormal vital signs and respiratory distress
options.C: A calm patient who smelled fumes outside a factory
options.D: A patient with a mild skin redness on one hand

explanation: If vital signs are crashing and the patient is struggling to breathe, they need immediate, high-priority emergency care. [learn more](GNS215_U5_T5#GNS215_U5_T5_h6)

question: Why must you give careful discharge advice to a chemical exposure patient who currently looks and feels completely fine?

options.A: Some chemical injuries and pulmonary complications develop hours later
options.B: Most chemical exposures become contagious after twenty-four hours
options.C: Delayed blood tests are legally required to be performed at home
options.D: Hospital policy requires patients to read safety manuals at home

explanation: Some poisons play the long game. Tissue damage can pop up hours after the exposure, so patients need to know what warning signs to watch for at home. [learn more](GNS215_U5_T5#GNS215_U5_T5_h6)

question: What is the very first priority when caring for a patient with acute poisoning?

options.A: Injecting the specific antidote
options.B: Drawing blood for toxicology
options.C: Administering activated charcoal
options.D: Securing the airway

explanation: Patient resuscitation always starts with the ABCs, making airway patency the absolute first priority before any other intervention. [learn more](GNS215_U5_T6#GNS215_U5_T6_h1)

question: Why is a full physical check with clothing removed necessary for a poisoned patient?

options.A: To find hidden transdermal patches or chemical spills
options.B: To check for signs of chronic nutritional deficiencies
options.C: To prepare the patient for immediate surgical intervention
options.D: To calculate the exact body surface area for drug dosing

explanation: Removing clothing allows nurses to discover concealed toxins like patches or corrosives that continue to cause harm if left in contact with the skin. [learn more](GNS215_U5_T6#GNS215_U5_T6_h1)

question: What four core details must a nurse gather regarding the poisoning event?

options.A: Weight, height, age, and blood type
options.B: Substance, amount, time, and route
options.C: Religion, occupation, tribe, and address
options.D: Pulse rate, temperature, respiration, and pain

explanation: Knowing what, how much, when, and how the poison entered the body dictates the entire direction of emergency medical care. [learn more](GNS215_U5_T6#GNS215_U5_T6_h2)

question: A patient with pinpoint pupils, slow breathing, and drowsiness arrives at the ward. What clinical term describes recognizing this specific pattern of signs?

options.A: Pain intensity rating
options.B: Toxidrome recognition
options.C: Neurological reflex testing
options.D: Nutritional screening

explanation: A toxidrome is a group of signs and symptoms that points toward a specific class of poisons, such as opioids in this case. [learn more](GNS215_U5_T6#GNS215_U5_T6_h2)

question: Which substance is commonly used to bind toxins in the gut and prevent their absorption?

options.A: Magnesium hydroxide
options.B: Activated charcoal
options.C: Normal saline solution
options.D: Liquid paraffin oil

explanation: Activated charcoal has a vast surface area that binds numerous poisons, preventing them from crossing the gastrointestinal mucosal barrier into the bloodstream. [learn more](GNS215_U5_T6#GNS215_U5_T6_h3)

question: What is a major risk of performing gastric lavage (stomach washout) on a poisoned patient?

options.A: Permanent staining of the digestive tract lining
options.B: High risk of aspiration and stomach perforation
options.C: Immediate neutralization of all available emergency antidotes
options.D: Complete inability to remove liquid poisons from the body

explanation: Gastric lavage is an invasive procedure that can push stomach contents into the lungs or tear the stomach wall, so its risks often outweigh benefits. [learn more](GNS215_U5_T6#GNS215_U5_T6_h3)

question: Which medical procedure uses a machine to filter toxins directly from a patient's blood?

options.A: Gastric lavage
options.B: Urinary alkalinization
options.C: Enteral nutrition
options.D: Hemodialysis

explanation: Hemodialysis effectively removes small, water-soluble toxins and corrects severe acid-base disturbances by filtering the blood externally. [learn more](GNS215_U5_T6#GNS215_U5_T6_h4)

question: How does urinary alkalinization help clear weak acid poisons like aspirin from the body?

options.A: By stimulating the liver to break down the toxin into harmless gas
options.B: By trapping ionized drug molecules in the kidney tubules to prevent reabsorption
options.C: By increasing how fast the stomach empties into the small intestines
options.D: By neutralizing body acidity directly inside the bone marrow

explanation: Making the urine alkaline turns weak acids into a form that cannot cross back across cell membranes into the bloodstream, helping the body pass them out. [learn more](GNS215_U5_T6#GNS215_U5_T6_h4)

question: What is the specific antidote administered for an acute paracetamol (acetaminophen) overdose?

options.A: N-acetylcysteine
options.B: Naloxone hydrochloride
options.C: Calcium gluconate
options.D: Atropine sulfate

explanation: N-acetylcysteine replenishes hepatic glutathione stores, protecting the liver from toxic metabolites produced during paracetamol breakdown. [learn more](GNS215_U5_T6#GNS215_U5_T6_h5)

question: What common misconception do some healthcare workers hold regarding the treatment of poisoning?

options.A: Believing a specific antidote exists for every known poison
options.B: Trusting that urine alkalinization works for all drug classes
options.C: Expecting activated charcoal to cure heavy metal poisoning
options.D: Thinking that gastric lavage is safe at any given time

explanation: Specific antidotes are available for only a small number of toxins, making general supportive care the true foundation of toxicology management. [learn more](GNS215_U5_T6#GNS215_U5_T6_h5)

question: What is the primary goal of supportive care for a patient with acute poisoning?

options.A: Maintaining vital organ function until the body clears the toxin
options.B: Preventing the patient from sleeping throughout admission
options.C: Completely removing the poison from the body within one hour
options.D: Administering multiple different antidotes at the same time

explanation: Supportive care bridges the gap by keeping body systems functioning while natural processes eliminate the offending substance. [learn more](GNS215_U5_T6#GNS215_U5_T6_h6)

question: A patient poisoned by an organophosphate insecticide starts having generalized seizures. What medication should the nurse expect to give immediately?

options.A: Furosemide
options.B: Diazepam
options.C: Paracetamol
options.D: Adrenaline

explanation: Benzodiazepines like diazepam are the frontline drugs used to stop seizures and prevent further brain injury. [learn more](GNS215_U5_T6#GNS215_U5_T6_h6)

question: Why is monitoring urine output essential in patients recovering from severe poisoning?

options.A: To calculate daily vitamin requirements
options.B: To measure exact daily food intake
options.C: To determine the patient's blood group
options.D: To evaluate and protect kidney function

explanation: Many toxins and their breakdown products can cause direct kidney damage, making urine output a key sign of renal health. [learn more](GNS215_U5_T6#GNS215_U5_T6_h7)

question: What essential evaluation must happen before discharging a patient admitted for an intentional drug overdose?

options.A: Full blood lipid profile evaluation
options.B: Routine occupational therapy assessment
options.C: Comprehensive reflex testing
options.D: Psychiatric assessment for self-harm risk

explanation: Intentional overdoses stem from psychological distress, requiring mental health evaluation and support to keep the patient safe. [learn more](GNS215_U5_T6#GNS215_U5_T6_h7)

question: What is the main job of an antidote in poisoning cases?

options.A: A substance that neutralizes or counteracts a poison
options.B: A routine supplement given to boost immunity
options.C: A medication that cures all known drug overdoses
options.D: A chemical that completely destroys red blood cells

explanation: Think of an antidote as the specific counter-punch to a toxin. It is designed to bind to or neutralize harmful substances in the body. You've got this! [learn more](GNS215_U5_T7#GNS215_U5_T7_h1)

question: Why do patients still need supportive care (like IV fluids and oxygen) even after getting an antidote?

options.A: Antidotes usually worsen the patient's baseline vital signs
options.B: Supportive care keeps the patient stable while the body handles the toxin
options.C: Supportive care replaces the need for any toxicological screening
options.D: Antidotes are completely ineffective without continuous intravenous fluids

explanation: Antidotes are amazing, but they aren't instant magic. Supportive care keeps the patient breathing and stable while the antidote and the body do the heavy lifting to clear the poison. [learn more](GNS215_U5_T7#GNS215_U5_T7_h1)

question: How do chelating agents work to clear heavy metal poisoning?

options.A: By blocking nerve receptors in the central nervous system
options.B: By binding to metal ions to form complexes for renal excretion
options.C: By speeding up liver enzymes to break down fat stores
options.D: By increasing the production of red blood cells in bone marrow

explanation: Chelators act like little chemical handcuffs. They wrap around heavy metals to form a safe compound that your kidneys can easily flush out in the urine. [learn more](GNS215_U5_T7#GNS215_U5_T7_h2)

question: What is the main goal of a receptor antagonist antidote?

options.A: To coat the intestinal lining and prevent food digestion
options.B: To occupy the same receptor sites and block the toxin from attaching
options.C: To destroy the toxin molecule directly inside the stomach
options.D: To stimulate the liver to store extra glucose for energy

explanation: An antagonist gets to the parking spot (receptor) first and refuses to leave, blocking the toxin from parking there and causing trouble! [learn more](GNS215_U5_T7#GNS215_U5_T7_h2)

question: Which specific antidote is given for a paracetamol (acetaminophen) overdose?

options.A: Activated charcoal
options.B: Protamine sulfate
options.C: Naloxone hydrochloride
options.D: N-acetylcysteine

explanation: N-acetylcysteine (often called NAC) is the lifesaving go-to for paracetamol overdoses. It restores liver protectors (glutathione) just in time to save the liver cells. [learn more](GNS215_U5_T7#GNS215_U5_T7_h3)

question: A patient is rushed in with pinpoint pupils, severe sleepiness, and very slow breathing after a drug overdose. Which antidote do you expect the doctor to order?

options.A: Atropine
options.B: Flumazenil
options.C: Naloxone
options.D: Calcium gluconate

explanation: Pinpoint pupils and shallow, slow breathing are classic red flags for an opioid overdose. Naloxone quickly reverses these dangerous effects. [learn more](GNS215_U5_T7#GNS215_U5_T7_h3)

question: Why is it so crucial to give an antidote as early as possible?

options.A: It shortens the hospital stay to exactly twelve hours
options.B: It guarantees the patient will experience zero side effects
options.C: It completely eliminates the need for any laboratory blood tests
options.D: It prevents the toxin from causing irreversible organ damage

explanation: Time is tissue! Giving the antidote early stops the poison from locking onto vital organs and doing permanent harm. [learn more](GNS215_U5_T7#GNS215_U5_T7_h4)

question: What is the main danger of waiting for lab test results before treating certain severe poisonings?

options.A: Immediate kidney failure from drawing too much blood
options.B: Severe allergic reactions to the laboratory reagents
options.C: Automatic rejection of insurance claims by the hospital
options.D: Dangerous delays in giving life-saving therapy

explanation: In toxicology emergencies, clinical signs matter more than paperwork. Waiting on lab results can waste precious time while the poison takes over. [learn more](GNS215_U5_T7#GNS215_U5_T7_h4)

question: In a life-threatening poisoning emergency, which route of administration is generally preferred for antidotes?

options.A: Intravenous
options.B: Transdermal
options.C: Subcutaneous
options.D: Rectal suppository

explanation: The IV route puts the antidote straight into the bloodstream so it can start working almost immediately when every second counts. [learn more](GNS215_U5_T7#GNS215_U5_T7_h5)

question: How are many antidote doses managed during emergency treatment?

options.A: Calculated using the hospital room number and time of day
options.B: Decreased by half every hour regardless of symptoms
options.C: Titrated carefully against the patient's ongoing clinical response
options.D: Fixed permanently based solely on the patient's age in years

explanation: Every patient reacts differently to poisons. Nurses and doctors watch the patient's vital signs and symptoms closely, adjusting the drug dose up or down as needed. [learn more](GNS215_U5_T7#GNS215_U5_T7_h5)

question: Why must nurses continue monitoring a patient long after the first dose of an antidote is given?

options.A: Antidotes always cause permanent damage to the endocrine system
options.B: The toxin may outlast the antidote and cause symptoms to return
options.C: Patients usually try to escape from the hospital unassisted
options.D: Laboratory monitors automatically shut down after four hours

explanation: Sometimes an antidote wears off before the poison is fully cleared from the body. Continuous monitoring ensures the patient doesn't suddenly slip back into toxicity. [learn more](GNS215_U5_T7#GNS215_U5_T7_h6)

question: Which of these options is NOT something a nurse needs to track after giving an antidote?

options.A: Daily shoe size and foot width measurements
options.B: Continuous vital signs and breathing patterns
options.C: Relevant laboratory markers and blood gas results
options.D: Neurological alertness and mental status

explanation: Your patient's shoe size won't tell you how they are recovering from poison! Breathing, alertness, and lab results are what truly matter. [learn more](GNS215_U5_T7#GNS215_U5_T7_h6)

question: What is an essential nursing duty when caring for a patient with acute poisoning?

options.A: Leaving the patient alone to rest quietly in a dark room
options.B: Gathering the history, securing samples, and keeping the bedside safe
options.C: Disposing of all empty medication containers immediately
options.D: Prescribing the final discharge medications without doctor review

explanation: Nurses act as detectives! Collecting pill bottles, noting what was taken, and keeping the patient safe from harm are key parts of emergency care. [learn more](GNS215_U5_T7#GNS215_U5_T7_h7)

question: A patient is physically stable after recovering from an intentional overdose. What is the most important next step in their care?

options.A: Discharge the patient immediately with a warning never to return
options.B: Scold the patient for wasting hospital resources and staff time
options.C: Arrange for a mental health evaluation and ongoing psychological support
options.D: Assume the underlying issue is resolved and stop all observation

explanation: Physical healing is only half the battle. For intentional self-harm, a psychiatric assessment and emotional support before discharge are essential for keeping the patient safe. [learn more](GNS215_U5_T7#GNS215_U5_T7_h7)

question: How do airborne gases and fumes mostly enter the body?

options.A: Parenteral injection
options.B: Dermal absorption
options.C: Inhalation
options.D: Ingestion

explanation: Airborne fumes and gases enter through the respiratory tract and quickly cross into the bloodstream. [learn more](GNS215_U5_T8#GNS215_U5_T8_h1)

question: A chemical splashes onto a worker's bare skin. What type of exposure is this?

options.A: Inhalation exposure
options.B: Mucosal ingestion
options.C: Dermal absorption
options.D: Subcutaneous injection

explanation: Direct contact with the skin allows chemicals to pass through the outer layers into the body. [learn more](GNS215_U5_T8#GNS215_U5_T8_h1)

question: Which chemical substance causes the most acute poisoning cases among rural farmers?

options.A: Inactivated viral vaccines
options.B: Water-soluble vitamins
options.C: Organophosphate pesticides
options.D: Non-steroidal anti-inflammatories

explanation: Farmers frequently use organophosphates for pest control, making them a common cause of agricultural poisoning. [learn more](GNS215_U5_T8#GNS215_U5_T8_h2)

question: In many homes, accidental poisoning often happens because dangerous liquids are stored in what type of container?

options.A: Empty soft drink bottles
options.B: Sealed medical sterile packs
options.C: Heavy-duty lead-lined drums
options.D: Certified chemical carboys

explanation: Using old beverage bottles for household chemicals like kerosene confuses children and adults, leading to accidental swallowing. [learn more](GNS215_U5_T8#GNS215_U5_T8_h2)

question: What is the main goal of primary prevention in chemical safety?

options.A: Rehabilitating chronic organ damage
options.B: Stopping exposure before it occurs
options.C: Treating symptoms after poisoning happens
options.D: Administering specific antidotes quickly

explanation: Primary prevention focuses on stopping contact with toxic substances before any exposure happens. [learn more](GNS215_U5_T8#GNS215_U5_T8_h3)

question: Why should you never store chemicals near food supplies?

options.A: It accelerates the expiration date of the food
options.B: It attracts unwanted rodents to the storage room
options.C: It alters the chemical pH levels instantly
options.D: It prevents accidental cross-contamination and ingestion

explanation: Keeping chemicals away from food stops them from leaking or mixing into what we eat or drink. [learn more](GNS215_U5_T8#GNS215_U5_T8_h3)

question: How is personal protective equipment (PPE) classified when dealing with workplace hazards?

options.A: The primary substitution
options.B: The administrative control
options.C: The environmental elimination
options.D: The final barrier

explanation: PPE is the last line of defense when other safety measures fail to remove the hazard. [learn more](GNS215_U5_T8#GNS215_U5_T8_h4)

question: What protective gear should a worker handling strong acids wear to prevent skin burns?

options.A: Open-toe leather safety boots
options.B: Chemical-resistant gloves and aprons
options.C: Standard cotton overalls and caps
options.D: Disposable surgical face masks

explanation: Acids require special waterproof materials like rubber to stop them from burning the skin. [learn more](GNS215_U5_T8#GNS215_U5_T8_h4)

question: What is the immediate first-aid action if a chemical splashes into a person's eyes?

options.A: Applying dry sterile gauze pads tightly
options.B: Waiting for specialist ophthalmologist review
options.C: Flushing continuously with clean water
options.D: Administering systemic oral analgesics

explanation: Washing the eyes with plenty of water dilutes and removes the chemical before it can damage the cornea. [learn more](GNS215_U5_T8#GNS215_U5_T8_h5)

question: Why is removing contaminated clothing so important during emergency care for poisoning?

options.A: It stops ongoing dermal absorption of the chemical
options.B: It reduces the financial cost of medical treatment
options.C: It prevents staining of clinical examination couches
options.D: It prepares the patient for routine hospital laundry

explanation: Clothes soaked in chemicals keep the toxin in contact with the skin until they are taken off. [learn more](GNS215_U5_T8#GNS215_U5_T8_h5)

question: Which Nigerian agency is responsible for regulating chemical safety and product labeling?

options.A: NEPA
options.B: FRSC
options.C: NAFDAC
options.D: JAMB

explanation: NAFDAC regulates the manufacture, importation, and distribution of chemicals and drugs in Nigeria. [learn more](GNS215_U5_T8#GNS215_U5_T8_h6)

question: How do community health nurses help with local toxicology surveillance?

options.A: Prosecuting illegal chemical manufacturing plants
options.B: Manufacturing pharmaceutical antidote supplies
options.C: Formulating new industrial safety legislation
options.D: Reporting unusual clusters of poisoning cases

explanation: Nurses notice unusual health trends in the community and report them so authorities can act quickly. [learn more](GNS215_U5_T8#GNS215_U5_T8_h6)

question: What broad category of cellular structure do parasites share with human hosts?

options.A: Viral
options.B: Prokaryotic
options.C: Mycotic
options.D: Eukaryotic

explanation: Parasites are eukaryotic organisms, which means their cells contain a nucleus and organelles similar to human cells. [learn more](GNS215_U6_T1#GNS215_U6_T1_h1)

question: Why is developing drugs against parasites more difficult than creating antibacterial agents?

options.A: Bacterial infections are always easier to diagnose in clinics
options.B: Antiparasitic drugs cannot be administered through oral routes
options.C: Parasites reproduce much faster than human bacterial cells
options.D: Parasitic cells closely resemble human cells in structure

explanation: The similarity between human and parasitic cells makes achieving selective toxicity difficult without harming the host. [learn more](GNS215_U6_T1#GNS215_U6_T1_h1)

question: Mebendazole primarily kills intestinal worms by interfering with which parasite process?

options.A: Red blood cell oxygen transport
options.B: Microtubule synthesis and glucose uptake
options.C: Bacterial cell wall formation
options.D: Calcium ion channel regulation

explanation: Benzimidazoles disrupt cellular structures called microtubules, stopping the worm from absorbing glucose and surviving. [learn more](GNS215_U6_T1#GNS215_U6_T1_h2)

question: How does Praziquantel cause the destruction of flatworms and tapeworms?

options.A: By destroying the outer protective cell wall of bacteria
options.B: By blocking folic acid synthesis in the parasite gut
options.C: By stopping the replication of viral genetic material
options.D: By increasing calcium permeability and causing paralysis

explanation: Praziquantel shifts calcium balance inside the worm, inducing tetanic muscle contractions followed by paralysis. [learn more](GNS215_U6_T1#GNS215_U6_T1_h2)

question: What is the current first-line treatment recommendation for uncomplicated falciparum malaria?

options.A: Intravenous quinine infusion therapy
options.B: Artemisinin-based combination therapy
options.C: Long-term primaquine daily dosing
options.D: Standard oral chloroquine monotherapy

explanation: ACTs are recommended globally as the primary treatment to clear parasites quickly and prevent treatment failure. [learn more](GNS215_U6_T1#GNS215_U6_T1_h3)

question: A patient treated for Plasmodium vivax malaria requires which specific drug to prevent future disease relapses from liver hypnozoites?

options.A: Primaquine
options.B: Artesunate
options.C: Quinine
options.D: Chloroquine

explanation: Primaquine is uniquely effective at clearing dormant liver-stage parasites responsible for the relapse of vivax malaria. [learn more](GNS215_U6_T1#GNS215_U6_T1_h3)

question: Metronidazole exerts its therapeutic effect against protozoa primarily by damaging which cellular component?

options.A: Ribosomes
options.B: Cell wall
options.C: DNA
options.D: Microtubules

explanation: Metronidazole is reduced inside the organism to reactive intermediates that cause breakage of microbial and protozoal DNA strands. [learn more](GNS215_U6_T1#GNS215_U6_T1_h4)

question: Which instruction is critical for a patient prescribed oral metronidazole for trichomoniasis?

options.A: Stop the prescription immediately when symptoms resolve
options.B: Avoid consuming alcohol during and immediately after therapy
options.C: Expose skin to direct sunlight to activate the drug
options.D: Take the medication exclusively on an empty stomach with milk

explanation: Metronidazole causes a severe disulfiram-like reaction when mixed with alcohol, leading to flushing, nausea, and severe vomiting. [learn more](GNS215_U6_T1#GNS215_U6_T1_h4)

question: Permethrin cream works against scabies mites by disrupting which physiological mechanism?

options.A: Sodium ion channels in nerve membranes
options.B: Cell wall synthesis in the mite exoskeleton
options.C: Folic acid production inside the gut
options.D: Calcium uptake in muscle tissues

explanation: Permethrin disrupts voltage-gated sodium channels, leading to paralysis and death of the scabies mite. [learn more](GNS215_U6_T1#GNS215_U6_T1_h5)

question: A patient treated for a scabies infestation asks when skin itching will completely stop. What is the best nursing response?

options.A: New itching indicates a bacterial superinfection has started
options.B: Antihistamines should be stopped immediately to speed up healing
options.C: Itching may persist for several weeks even after the mites are dead
options.D: Continued itching proves the treatment failed and must be repeated

explanation: Post-scabietic pruritus is common due to an ongoing allergic reaction to dead mites and their waste products under the skin. [learn more](GNS215_U6_T1#GNS215_U6_T1_h5)

question: Why is gastrointestinal upset a common side effect for almost all classes of antiparasitic drugs?

options.A: Interference with pancreatic enzyme release in the duodenum
options.B: Local irritation and the systemic breakdown of parasites in the body
options.C: Their primary action on human gastric acid production cells
options.D: The requirement that all these medications be taken without water

explanation: Gastrointestinal symptoms stem from direct mucosal irritation by the drugs and the inflammatory response to dying parasites. [learn more](GNS215_U6_T1#GNS215_U6_T1_h6)

question: Which of the following laboratory parameters should be monitored during prolonged albendazole or mebendazole therapy? (Select the best match)

options.A: Serum creatinine and random blood glucose
options.B: Liver function tests and complete blood count
options.C: Thyroid stimulating hormone and lipid profile
options.D: Coagulation profiles and electrolyte levels

explanation: Prolonged use of benzimidazoles carries a risk of hepatotoxicity and bone marrow suppression, necessitating periodic blood work. [learn more](GNS215_U6_T1#GNS215_U6_T1_h6)

question: What is the primary difference between antiseptics and disinfectants?

options.A: Antiseptics are heat-based methods while disinfectants are chemical solutions
options.B: Antiseptics are used on living tissue while disinfectants are used on inanimate objects
options.C: Disinfectants destroy all spores instantly whereas antiseptics only kill viruses
options.D: Disinfectants are safe for human skin but antiseptics are toxic

explanation: The key distinction is the target surface; living tissue requires milder agents, while non-living surfaces tolerate harsher chemicals. [learn more](GNS215_U6_T10#GNS215_U6_T10_h1)

question: A nurse uses a concentrated surface disinfectant to clean a patient's skin wound. What is the most likely outcome?

options.A: Complete eradication of skin flora with no adverse effects
options.B: Chemical burns and tissue damage
options.C: Rapid healing without scarring
options.D: Incomplete disinfection due to low potency

explanation: Surface disinfectants are too harsh for living cells and will damage human tissue. [learn more](GNS215_U6_T10#GNS215_U6_T10_h1)

question: How do alcohol-based antiseptics primarily destroy microorganisms?

options.A: By dissolving the cell wall with strong acids
options.B: By binding permanently to nucleic acids
options.C: By denaturing cellular proteins
options.D: By freezing the cytoplasm

explanation: Alcohols work by unfolding and precipitating vital proteins inside the microbial cell. [learn more](GNS215_U6_T10#GNS215_U6_T10_h2)

question: An agent that increases cell membrane permeability causes microbial death by what primary event?

options.A: Leakage of vital intracellular contents
options.B: Thickening of the outer capsule
options.C: Rapid acceleration of metabolic rate
options.D: Enhancement of nutrient absorption

explanation: When the membrane breaks down, essential molecules escape, leading to cell death. [learn more](GNS215_U6_T10#GNS215_U6_T10_h2)

question: Which chemical agent is commonly used for high-level disinfection of heat-sensitive medical equipment like endoscopes?

options.A: Normal saline
options.B: Isopropyl alcohol
options.C: Glutaraldehyde
options.D: Hydrogen peroxide 3%

explanation: Aldehydes like glutaraldehyde are potent enough for high-level disinfection of delicate instruments. [learn more](GNS215_U6_T10#GNS215_U6_T10_h3)

question: Chlorhexidine is frequently chosen for surgical hand scrubs because of which unique property?

options.A: It changes color when the skin is fully sterile
options.B: It neutralizes all known bacterial spores instantly upon contact
options.C: It provides persistent residual antimicrobial action on the skin
options.D: It evaporates rapidly without leaving any chemical residue

explanation: Chlorhexidine binds to the stratum corneum, offering prolonged protection against bacterial growth. [learn more](GNS215_U6_T10#GNS215_U6_T10_h3)

question: The presence of organic matter like blood or pus affects disinfection by doing what?

options.A: Inactivating or shielding the chemical agent
options.B: Enhancing penetration through cell walls
options.C: Accelerating the chemical reaction time
options.D: Converting the disinfectant into an antiseptic

explanation: Organic debris binds or blocks disinfectants, which is why cleaning must precede disinfection. [learn more](GNS215_U6_T10#GNS215_U6_T10_h4)

question: A nurse wipes down a treatment table with bleach and immediately dries it within five seconds. What went wrong?

options.A: Insufficient contact time
options.B: Excessive ambient temperature
options.C: Incompatible surface material
options.D: Incorrect chemical concentration

explanation: Disinfectants need adequate time sitting wet on a surface to fully eradicate pathogens. [learn more](GNS215_U6_T10#GNS215_U6_T10_h4)

question: Why is skin preparation for surgery performed by moving from the incision site outward?

options.A: To ensure the antiseptic dries faster in the center
options.B: To push contaminated flora away from the clean surgical area
options.C: To cover a larger surface area with less antiseptic
options.D: To keep the peripheral skin dry while prepping

explanation: Moving from clean to dirty prevents dragging outer skin bacteria toward the sterile wound site. [learn more](GNS215_U6_T10#GNS215_U6_T10_h5)

question: Which nursing action is essential when preparing chemical disinfectant solutions for instrument soaking?

options.A: Storing the active solution in an open basin
options.B: Verifying the correct dilution ratio and expiration date
options.C: Mixing multiple disinfectant brands for maximum potency
options.D: Heating the solution to boiling point before immersion

explanation: Accurate dilution and fresh solutions ensure the chemical retains its intended antimicrobial strength. [learn more](GNS215_U6_T10#GNS215_U6_T10_h5)

question: Inhalation of volatile fumes from strong disinfectants like glutaraldehyde primarily causes irritation to which body system?

options.A: Gastrointestinal tract
options.B: Cardiovascular system
options.C: Respiratory tract
options.D: Central nervous system

explanation: Strong chemical fumes irritate the airways, leading to coughing, wheezing, and mucosal damage. [learn more](GNS215_U6_T10#GNS215_U6_T10_h6)

question: Which of the following is NOT a recommended safety practice when handling toxic hospital disinfectants?

options.A: Ensuring adequate ventilation in the utility room
options.B: Wearing heavy-duty utility gloves and aprons
options.C: Storing mixed solutions in unmarked beverage bottles
options.D: Following manufacturer guidelines for proper dilution

explanation: Using beverage containers for chemicals creates a severe risk of accidental ingestion and poisoning. [learn more](GNS215_U6_T10#GNS215_U6_T10_h6)

question: What is the main difference between a standard IV infusion and a blood transfusion?

options.A: Transfusions never require a special intravenous line
options.B: Infusions are always given faster than blood transfusions
options.C: Infusions can only use blood products while transfusions use plain water
options.D: Infusions deliver fluids or medications while transfusions replace blood components

explanation: You've got this! Regular IV fluids give water, salts, or drugs, while blood transfusions specifically replace parts of the blood like red cells or plasma. Simple and clear! [learn more](GNS215_U6_T11#GNS215_U6_T11_h1)

question: Why do nurses need to be extra careful when giving IV fluids or blood products?

options.A: Patients always feel severe pain when any fluid enters a vein
options.B: Every procedure carries inherent risks such as fluid overload or severe reactions
options.C: Intravenous lines are guaranteed to clog within one hour
options.D: Hospital management requires extra paperwork for all fluid bags

explanation: Even though giving fluids is an everyday task, putting anything straight into the bloodstream can cause rapid changes or reactions. Staying alert keeps our patients safe! [learn more](GNS215_U6_T11#GNS215_U6_T11_h1)

question: What is the main feature of crystalloid IV solutions like normal saline?

options.A: They consist of massive protein structures that stay trapped in blood vessels
options.B: They can only be administered through central venous catheters
options.C: They are harvested directly from human blood donors
options.D: They contain small molecules that easily cross membranes into body tissues

explanation: Think of crystalloids as small-molecule solutions that easily move out of the blood vessels and into the tissues. Great concept to keep in mind for your ward postings! [learn more](GNS215_U6_T11#GNS215_U6_T11_h2)

question: Which blood product is best to give a patient who is bleeding heavily because they lack clotting factors?

options.A: 5% Dextrose in water
options.B: Normal Saline solution
options.C: Fresh Frozen Plasma
options.D: Packed Red Blood Cells

explanation: Fresh Frozen Plasma is packed with the vital clotting factors needed to help stop bleeding. You're building great clinical judgment! [learn more](GNS215_U6_T11#GNS215_U6_T11_h2)

question: Which IV solution is the ONLY safe one to hang alongside a blood transfusion?

options.A: 0.9% Sodium Chloride
options.B: 0.45% Sodium Chloride
options.C: Lactated Ringer's Solution
options.D: 5% Dextrose in Water

explanation: Normal saline (0.9% NaCl) plays nice with blood! Other fluids like dextrose can cause red blood cells to burst (hemolysis), while Ringer's has calcium that can cause clotting in the tubing. [learn more](GNS215_U6_T11#GNS215_U6_T11_h3)

question: Why is a bedside double-check with two nurses a must before starting a blood transfusion?

options.A: To make sure the nurse finishes the shift on time
options.B: To prevent fatal errors by confirming exact patient and blood product matching
options.C: To measure the exact weight of the blood bag before hanging
options.D: To ensure the blood pump is plugged into a backup generator

explanation: Two pairs of eyes are better than one! Checking details together ensures the right blood goes to the right patient every single time. [learn more](GNS215_U6_T11#GNS215_U6_T11_h3)

question: How long should a nurse stay right by the patient's side after a blood transfusion starts?

options.A: Only until the pump is turned on
options.B: The first 15 minutes
options.C: Until the entire bag is empty
options.D: The first two hours

explanation: Most serious transfusion reactions happen fast at the very beginning. Staying close for those first 15 minutes lets you catch and treat any reaction early! [learn more](GNS215_U6_T11#GNS215_U6_T11_h4)

question: What is the main reason a bag of blood must be completely infused within four hours?

options.A: To ensure the infusion pump battery does not run out of power
options.B: To prevent dangerous bacterial growth in the blood at room temperature
options.C: To stop the patient from becoming too cold during the procedure
options.D: To prevent the red blood cells from settling at the bottom of the bag

explanation: Blood is warm and rich in nutrients—bacteria love it too! Finishing it within four hours stops germs from multiplying in the bag. [learn more](GNS215_U6_T11#GNS215_U6_T11_h4)

question: What is the VERY FIRST thing a nurse must do if a patient shows signs of a transfusion reaction?

options.A: Call the hospital maintenance team
options.B: Administer an oral pain reliever
options.C: Slow down the infusion pump rate
options.D: Stop the transfusion immediately

explanation: Safety first! Stopping the flow immediately keeps any more of the incompatible blood from entering their body. You're thinking like a real nurse! [learn more](GNS215_U6_T11#GNS215_U6_T11_h5)

question: A patient having a blood transfusion suddenly develops fever, chills, and sharp lower back pain. What is likely happening?

options.A: Delayed iron toxicity
options.B: Circulatory fluid overload
options.C: Simple allergic skin rash
options.D: Acute hemolytic reaction

explanation: Lower back pain, fever, and chills are classic warning signs that the body is reacting against the red blood cells. Great clinical cue to remember! [learn more](GNS215_U6_T11#GNS215_U6_T11_h5)

question: What is the main reason we apply most topical drugs to the skin?

options.A: To bypass the digestive tract entirely for rapid blood concentration
options.B: To achieve a localized effect at the application site
options.C: To provide systemic nutrition through the skin
options.D: To replace intravenous therapy in emergency resuscitation

explanation: You've got this! Topical medications are designed to work right where you put them, treating local skin issues without flooding the whole body with medicine. [learn more](GNS215_U6_T12#GNS215_U6_T12_h1)

question: Why might you need to watch a patient for whole-body (systemic) effects after applying a topical cream or patch?

options.A: Skin application always causes widespread allergic reactions.
options.B: Topical drugs change the local skin temperature, affecting blood pressure.
options.C: Some topical agents are designed to cross the skin barrier and enter the bloodstream.
options.D: All topical drugs automatically travel to the liver first before working.

explanation: Spot on! While many stay local, formulations like transdermal patches are specially made to pass through the skin into the bloodstream to heal the whole body. [learn more](GNS215_U6_T12#GNS215_U6_T12_h1)

question: Which layer of the skin acts as the toughest bodyguard against drug absorption?

options.A: Stratum corneum
options.B: Basal cell layer
options.C: Dermis
options.D: Subcutaneous layer

explanation: Great job! The stratum corneum is the outermost layer made of tough, dead cells and lipids that tightly guards what is allowed to pass into our bodies. [learn more](GNS215_U6_T12#GNS215_U6_T12_h2)

question: A patient has severe burns on their chest. Why does putting medicated cream here put them at risk for drug overload?

options.A: Burns block all local blood flow, causing the drug to pool dangerously under the skin.
options.B: Burned skin traps the medication and forces it to travel directly to the liver.
options.C: The protective stratum corneum is damaged, allowing rapid and excessive drug entry into the bloodstream.
options.D: Damaged skin cells chemically react with the cream to create new toxins.

explanation: You're learning fast! When burns or wounds damage the skin's outer guard layer, too much medicine can rush into the bloodstream all at once. [learn more](GNS215_U6_T12#GNS215_U6_T12_h2)

question: Which type of topical treatment is best for treating a stubborn, thick, dry patch of skin?

options.A: Aqueous solution
options.B: Ointment
options.C: Lotion
options.D: Gel

explanation: Ointments are oil-based and heavy, making them champs at locking in moisture and softening thick, dry skin. Keep up the good work! [learn more](GNS215_U6_T12#GNS215_U6_T12_h3)

question: A doctor prescribes a topical medication for a patient's oily, acne-prone face. Which form will you most likely give them?

options.A: Heavy cream
options.B: Emollient butter
options.C: Ointment
options.D: Gel

explanation: Gels are water- or alcohol-based and dry quickly without adding extra grease—perfect for oily skin and acne! [learn more](GNS215_U6_T12#GNS215_U6_T12_h3)

question: What is the main job of topical corticosteroids in skin care?

options.A: Numbing localized nerve pain
options.B: Hydrating dry skin scales
options.C: Killing superficial bacterial infections
options.D: Reducing inflammation and immune response

explanation: Spot on! Steroid creams are our go-to tools to calm down swelling, redness, and nagging itching from skin allergies and rashes. [learn more](GNS215_U6_T12#GNS215_U6_T12_h4)

question: What can happen if strong corticosteroid creams are used on thin skin areas for too long?

options.A: Permanent darkening of the hair follicles
options.B: Skin thinning and atrophy
options.C: Sudden systemic bacterial infection
options.D: Complete numbness of the local nerves

explanation: Using strong steroids for too long breaks down the skin's collagen, causing it to thin out. That's why we always follow prescription timelines carefully! [learn more](GNS215_U6_T12#GNS215_U6_T12_h4)

question: When giving eye drops, where is the safest spot to place the liquid?

options.A: Directly onto the center of the cornea
options.B: Into the lower conjunctival sac
options.C: Onto the upper eyelid surface
options.D: Into the inner corner tear duct

explanation: Dropping the medicine into the lower pocket keeps the delicate cornea safe from scratches while letting the drop spread evenly across the eye. [learn more](GNS215_U6_T12#GNS215_U6_T12_h5)

question: An adult patient needs ear drops for an infection. How should you pull their outer ear (auricle) to straighten the ear canal?

options.A: Pull the earlobe straight down toward the chin
options.B: Push the tragus forward tightly
options.C: Pull the auricle upward and outward
options.D: Tilt the entire head sideways without touching the ear

explanation: For adults, gently pulling the ear up and back straightens the canal so the drops flow all the way down smoothly. [learn more](GNS215_U6_T12#GNS215_U6_T12_h5)

question: What is the very first thing you should do before putting any topical medication on a patient's skin?

options.A: Massage the skin vigorously to increase blood flow
options.B: Apply a thick layer of petroleum jelly to protect surrounding tissue
options.C: Warm the cream under hot running water
options.D: Assess the condition and integrity of the target skin area

explanation: Always check the skin first! You need to make sure there are no unexpected cuts, open wounds, or signs of infection that would change your plan. [learn more](GNS215_U6_T12#GNS215_U6_T12_h6)

question: Why should you gently clean and dry the skin before applying a fresh layer of medicated cream?

options.A: To remove old medication residue, sweat, and dirt that could block proper absorption
options.B: To test if the patient's skin is sensitive to water
options.C: To permanently sterilize the skin surface against all bacteria
options.D: To open up the pores so the skin absorbs the entire tube at once

explanation: Cleaning clears away old cream and sweat barriers so the fresh medicine can make direct contact with the skin. [learn more](GNS215_U6_T12#GNS215_U6_T12_h6)

question: Why should you use a clean spatula or tongue depressor when taking cream from a shared jar?

options.A: To spread the cream faster across the patient's skin
options.B: To measure the exact milligram dose required
options.C: To warm the cream up before touching the patient
options.D: To prevent introducing bacteria and contaminating the jar

explanation: Using a tool instead of your bare fingers stops germs from getting into the shared jar and causing future infections. [learn more](GNS215_U6_T12#GNS215_U6_T12_h7)

question: A patient is prescribed a new transdermal patch for chest pain. What is a crucial step before putting on the fresh patch?

options.A: Remove the old transdermal patch from the previous site
options.B: Scrub the new site with alcohol until it bleeds
options.C: Apply an extra layer of steroid cream underneath the patch
options.D: Cover the new patch with airtight plastic wrap

explanation: Always take off the old patch first! Leaving it on alongside a new one can accidentally give the patient a dangerous drug overdose. [learn more](GNS215_U6_T12#GNS215_U6_T12_h7)

question: What is the most common local side effect of a topical skin medication?

options.A: Sudden kidney failure
options.B: Contact dermatitis and redness at the site
options.C: Complete hair loss on the scalp
options.D: Severe high blood pressure

explanation: Mild skin irritation, redness, or itching right where the cream was applied are the most common reactions to topical products. [learn more](GNS215_U6_T12#GNS215_U6_T12_h8)

question: When is a topical drug most likely to cause unexpected whole-body (systemic) side effects?

options.A: When stored at room temperature before application
options.B: When applied in a very thin layer on thick, calloused heels
options.C: When applied over large areas of broken or inflamed skin
options.D: When given to an adult instead of a child

explanation: You've got this! Large areas of wounded or inflamed skin let massive amounts of medicine sneak past the body's defenses into the bloodstream. [learn more](GNS215_U6_T12#GNS215_U6_T12_h8)

question: What key instruction should you give a patient about how much topical cream to use?

options.A: Mix all prescribed creams together to save time
options.B: Use only the exact prescribed amount in a thin layer
options.C: Stop applying the cream the moment the redness fades slightly
options.D: Apply as much as possible so it cures the condition faster

explanation: More isn't always better! Piling on extra cream doesn't speed up healing; it just increases the risk of skin irritation and unwanted side effects. [learn more](GNS215_U6_T12#GNS215_U6_T12_h9)

question: Why is it important to rotate where you stick daily patches or put long-term creams?

options.A: It stops the medication from expiring inside the body.
options.B: It keeps the skin color even across the whole body.
options.C: It ensures the medicine travels to all four limbs equally.
options.D: It prevents skin irritation, breakdown, and irritation from repetitive use in one spot.

explanation: Giving the skin a break by moving patches around prevents irritation, breakdown, and keeps the skin healthy enough to absorb the medicine properly. [learn more](GNS215_U6_T12#GNS215_U6_T12_h9)

question: Which specific immune cells does HIV attack and destroy in the body?

options.A: Neutrophils
options.B: Platelets
options.C: CD4+ T-lymphocytes
options.D: Red blood cells

explanation: Spot on! HIV goes straight for CD4+ T-lymphocytes, which are the commander cells of your immune system. Protecting them is key! [learn more](GNS215_U6_T13#GNS215_U6_T13_h1)

question: What is the main goal of giving antiretroviral therapy (ART) to someone with HIV?

options.A: To completely eliminate the virus from the body tissues
options.B: To lower the viral load and allow immune recovery
options.C: To prevent the transmission of common bacterial colds
options.D: To permanently repair damaged bone marrow cells

explanation: You got it! ART pushes the virus down to very low (undetectable) levels, giving your immune system the breathing room it needs to bounce back. [learn more](GNS215_U6_T13#GNS215_U6_T13_h1)

question: How do Nucleoside Reverse Transcriptase Inhibitors (NRTIs) help fight HIV?

options.A: They dissolve the fatty outer envelope of the virus
options.B: They act as faulty building blocks to stop viral DNA creation
options.C: They physically block the outer cell membrane receptors
options.D: They destroy mature viral particles circulating in the plasma

explanation: Brilliant! NRTIs act like fake Lego pieces. When the virus tries to build its DNA, it grabs the fake piece and the process grinds to a halt. [learn more](GNS215_U6_T13#GNS215_U6_T13_h2)

question: Why do doctors prescribe a combination of different HIV drugs instead of just one?

options.A: To eliminate the need for routine laboratory viral load testing
options.B: To ensure the patient has fewer daily pills to swallow
options.C: To completely cure the patient of the infection within weeks
options.D: To prevent the virus from quickly mutating and developing drug resistance

explanation: Exactly! Hitting the virus from multiple angles makes it super hard for it to mutate and find a way around the medication. [learn more](GNS215_U6_T13#GNS215_U6_T13_h2)

question: Which drug is a main part of the preferred first-line HIV treatment guidelines in Nigeria?

options.A: Dolutegravir
options.B: Ritonavir
options.C: Zidovudine
options.D: Nevirapine

explanation: Correct! Dolutegravir is a modern, highly effective drug that forms the backbone of standard first-line treatment today. [learn more](GNS215_U6_T13#GNS215_U6_T13_h3)

question: When should a nurse expect a patient to be switched to a second-line HIV regimen?

options.A: Whenever the patient experiences a mild common cold
options.B: As soon as the CD4 count climbs above normal levels
options.C: After the patient has taken the first drugs for exactly one year
options.D: When laboratory tests confirm persistent treatment failure

explanation: Spot on! We only switch regimens when lab results clearly show that the first set of drugs is no longer keeping the virus down. [learn more](GNS215_U6_T13#GNS215_U6_T13_h3)

question: What minimum percentage of adherence is needed for antiretroviral therapy to work successfully?
explanation: You nailed it! Patients need to take at least 95% of their doses on time to keep the virus suppressed and stop resistance. [learn more](GNS215_U6_T13#GNS215_U6_T13_h4)

question: Why is taking HIV medications right on schedule every single day so crucial?

options.A: Inconsistent timing causes permanent damage to the patient's liver enzymes
options.B: It ensures the pharmacy dispenses the correct refill amount each month
options.C: Missing doses lets drug levels drop, allowing the virus to mutate and resist the medication
options.D: Taking pills late instantly destroys all white blood cells in the body

explanation: Exactly! If drug levels in the blood drop too low, the virus wakes up, multiplies, and figures out how to fight off the drugs. [learn more](GNS215_U6_T13#GNS215_U6_T13_h4)

question: Which side effect is commonly linked to the long-term use of Tenofovir?

options.A: Sudden visual blindness
options.B: Kidney and bone toxicity
options.C: Severe permanent hair loss
options.D: Chronic high blood pressure
