explanation: Unlike anesthetics, analgesics reduce pain perception while allowing the patient to remain fully conscious. [learn more](GNS223_U5_T2#GNS223_U5_T2_h1)

question: Which common group of medications primarily blocks the production of prostaglandins?

options.A: Strong opioid drugs
options.B: Antidepressants
options.C: Brain sedatives
options.D: Non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs)

explanation: NSAIDs inhibit cyclooxygenase enzymes, which prevents the body from producing pain-promoting prostaglandins. [learn more](GNS223_U5_T2#GNS223_U5_T2_h2)

question: A patient with a history of severe stomach ulcers needs a painkiller. Which medication should the nurse avoid?

options.A: Oral diclofenac sodium tablets
options.B: Standard paracetamol tablets
options.C: A mild opioid combination syrup
options.D: Topical menthol cooling gel

explanation: NSAIDs like diclofenac damage the protective lining of the stomach, making them unsafe for patients with ulcers. [learn more](GNS223_U5_T2#GNS223_U5_T2_h2)

question: Which medication is given to quickly reverse slow breathing caused by an opioid overdose?

options.A: Adrenaline injection
options.B: Atropine sulfate
options.C: Diazepam solution
options.D: Naloxone hydrochloride

explanation: Naloxone is an opioid antagonist that quickly displaces opioids from receptors to restore normal breathing. [learn more](GNS223_U5_T2#GNS223_U5_T2_h3)

question: How do strong opioid medications primarily relieve moderate to severe pain?

options.A: By blocking peripheral enzyme pathways
options.B: By binding to receptors in the nervous system
options.C: By increasing serotonin levels in the spine
options.D: By numbing local tissue nerve endings

explanation: Opioids attach to specific receptors in the central and peripheral nervous system to block pain signals. [learn more](GNS223_U5_T2#GNS223_U5_T2_h3)

question: How is gabapentin mainly classified when used for pain management?

options.A: A muscle relaxant
options.B: A strong opioid agonist
options.C: A non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drug
options.D: An anticonvulsant used as an adjuvant pain med

explanation: Gabapentin is originally an anticonvulsant, but it works very well as an extra medication to manage nerve pain. [learn more](GNS223_U5_T2#GNS223_U5_T2_h4)

question: Which type of medication is most effective for treating nerve-related (neuropathic) pain?

options.A: High-dose fever reducers
options.B: Short-acting muscle relaxants
options.C: Local anesthetic skin patches
options.D: Adjuvant drugs like anticonvulsants

explanation: Nerve-related pain often does not respond to simple painkillers, so medications like anticonvulsants are added to help. [learn more](GNS223_U5_T2#GNS223_U5_T2_h4)

question: A patient has moderate cancer pain that is not relieved by basic non-opioid drugs. What should they receive next on the pain ladder?

options.A: A pure opioid antagonist drug
options.B: A weak opioid such as tramadol
options.C: Intravenous morphine immediately
options.D: A high-dose steroid alone

explanation: Step 2 of the WHO pain ladder introduces weak opioids when non-opioids are no longer enough to control pain. [learn more](GNS223_U5_T2#GNS223_U5_T2_h5)

question: What is the main goal of using the WHO analgesic ladder in clinical practice?

options.A: To ensure all patients eventually get strong intravenous narcotics
options.B: To provide a step-by-step guide for managing pain effectively
options.C: To replace all comfort measures with drugs
options.D: To restrict the use of paracetamol in elderly patients

explanation: The ladder gives nurses and doctors a clear, stepwise approach to choosing the right pain medication based on pain severity. [learn more](GNS223_U5_T2#GNS223_U5_T2_h5)

question: A patient taking regular oral morphine for severe pain has not had a bowel movement in four days. What should the nurse expect to do?

options.A: Start a prescribed laxative regimen
options.B: Stop all pain medication forever
options.C: Give an intravenous reversal drug
options.D: Switch the patient to aspirin

explanation: Opioids slow down bowel movements, so patients taking them regularly need laxatives to prevent severe constipation. [learn more](GNS223_U5_T2#GNS223_U5_T2_h6)

question: Which assessment is most important for a nurse to check before giving an intravenous opioid?

options.A: Leg muscle strength
options.B: Blood electrolyte levels
options.C: Respiratory rate and depth
options.D: Blood glucose level

explanation: Opioids can dangerously slow down breathing, so checking the patient's respiratory rate beforehand is a safety must. [learn more](GNS223_U5_T2#GNS223_U5_T2_h6)

question: Which enzyme do corticosteroids block to stop the body's inflammatory process?

options.A: Phospholipase A2
options.B: Cyclooxygenase-2
options.C: Acetylcholinesterase
options.D: Beta-lactamase

explanation: Spot on! Steroids block phospholipase A2 right at the beginning of the inflammation pathway, which stops inflammatory chemicals from ever forming. You've got this! [learn more](GNS223_U5_T3#GNS223_U5_T3_h1)

question: Why are corticosteroids much stronger at reducing inflammation than regular pain relievers?

options.A: They completely eliminate white blood cells.
options.B: They only target localized pain receptors in joints.
options.C: They act higher up the inflammatory chain by stopping chemical production at the source.
options.D: They work instantly within seconds to repair tissue.

explanation: Brilliant! Because they block the chain reaction right at the source (phospholipase A2), steroids have a powerful, whole-body anti-inflammatory effect. [learn more](GNS223_U5_T3#GNS223_U5_T3_h1)

question: Which of these medications is classified as a long-acting corticosteroid?

options.A: Prednisolone
options.B: Dexamethasone
options.C: Hydrocortisone
options.D: Methylprednisolone

explanation: Correct! Dexamethasone is a long-acting steroid that stays active in the body for 36 to 72 hours. Keep up the great revision! [learn more](GNS223_U5_T3#GNS223_U5_T3_h2)

question: What is the main difference between short-acting and long-acting corticosteroids?

options.A: How long they remain active in the body and their strength.
options.B: Whether they require a doctor's prescription.
options.C: If they cause weight gain during long-term therapy.
options.D: Whether they are swallowed or injected into a muscle.

explanation: You got it! Different steroid types stay in the system for different lengths of time and have varying strengths for reducing swelling. [learn more](GNS223_U5_T3#GNS223_U5_T3_h2)

question: Which route of administration is best for treating a sudden, life-threatening allergic reaction?

options.A: Inhaled powder
options.B: Oral tablet
options.C: Topical cream
options.D: Intravenous

explanation: Spot on! The intravenous (IV) route pushes the medication straight into the bloodstream for instant action during emergencies. [learn more](GNS223_U5_T3#GNS223_U5_T3_h3)

question: A patient with severe arthritis in one knee gets a direct steroid injection into the joint. What is the main benefit?

options.A: It lets the drug bypass the liver to enter the brain instantly.
options.B: It gives high drug concentration at the problem site while sparing the rest of the body.
options.C: It completely cures the underlying autoimmune disease.
options.D: It guarantees no side effects like high blood pressure.

explanation: Correct! Giving the injection right into the knee treats the local pain while keeping whole-body side effects as low as possible. [learn more](GNS223_U5_T3#GNS223_U5_T3_h3)

question: What is a major reason doctors prescribe corticosteroids for lung conditions?

options.A: To thin thick mucus so coughing is easier
options.B: To reduce airway swelling during severe asthma attacks
options.C: To kill bacterial germs inside the lungs
options.D: To lower high blood pressure in lung vessels

explanation: Well done! Steroids are powerful anti-inflammatory drugs that quickly open up swollen airways when an asthma attack strikes. [learn more](GNS223_U5_T3#GNS223_U5_T3_h4)

question: How do corticosteroids help patients with autoimmune diseases like lupus?

options.A: By calming an overactive immune system that is attacking healthy tissues
options.B: By destroying abnormal white blood cells in bone marrow
options.C: By rebuilding damaged joint cartilage and bone
options.D: By replacing lost vitamins in the blood

explanation: Spot on! In autoimmune conditions, the body attacks itself. Steroids act like a peacekeeper, calming down that overactive immune response. [learn more](GNS223_U5_T3#GNS223_U5_T3_h4)

question: Which of the following is a common long-term side effect of taking corticosteroids?

options.A: Permanently low blood pressure
options.B: Darkening of the skin tone
options.C: Rapid muscle building and weight loss
options.D: Osteoporosis and weak bones

explanation: Correct! Long-term steroid use messes with calcium and bone building, which can lead to fragile bones over time. Good clinical knowledge! [learn more](GNS223_U5_T3#GNS223_U5_T3_h5)

question: A patient taking high-dose prednisone for six months reports feeling very hungry all the time and notices weight gain around the face and neck. What causes this?

options.A: Fluid is building up inside the brain tissue.
options.B: Steroids alter how the body stores fat and stimulates appetite.
options.C: The medication is destroying the thyroid gland completely.
options.D: The patient is secretly eating too much junk food at night.

explanation: Corticosteroids alter carbohydrate and fat metabolism, frequently causing increased appetite and fat redistribution. [learn more](GNS223_U5_T3#GNS223_U5_T3_h5)

question: When should a nurse question a doctor's order to start systemic corticosteroid therapy?

options.A: When the patient has an active, untreated fungal infection
options.B: When the patient has stable, controlled blood pressure
options.C: When the patient had childhood asthma
options.D: When the patient has mild seasonal allergies

explanation: Spot on! Because steroids suppress the immune system, giving them during an active infection lets the infection run wild. Always check for infections first! [learn more](GNS223_U5_T3#GNS223_U5_T3_h6)

question: Why is taking corticosteroids together with NSAIDs (like ibuprofen) a big risk?

options.A: It causes blood pressure to drop dangerously low.
options.B: It cancels out the steroid so it doesn't work.
options.C: It greatly increases the chance of stomach ulcers and bleeding.
options.D: It stops the liver from filtering other drugs.

explanation: Brilliant! Both drugs irritate the stomach lining. Combining them multiplies the risk of painful ulcers and internal bleeding. [learn more](GNS223_U5_T3#GNS223_U5_T3_h6)

question: Which lab value or vital sign must be checked regularly for patients on long-term corticosteroids?

options.A: Liver enzyme AST
options.B: Blood glucose levels
options.C: Red blood cell count
options.D: Serum creatinine

explanation: Correct! Steroids trigger the liver to release stored sugar, which often leads to high blood sugar levels that need close monitoring. [learn more](GNS223_U5_T3#GNS223_U5_T3_h7)

question: Why is daily weight tracking so important for a patient taking oral prednisone?

options.A: It helps catch fluid retention and rapid water weight gain early.
options.B: It calculates the exact dose needed for the next day.
options.C: It proves the patient is absorbing pills through the stomach.
options.D: It ensures the patient is following a workout routine.

explanation: Spot on! Steroids cause the body to hold onto salt and water, making daily weigh-ins a great way to spot fluid overload early. [learn more](GNS223_U5_T3#GNS223_U5_T3_h7)

question: What life-threatening emergency can happen if a patient stops taking long-term steroids all of a sudden?

options.A: Heart attack
options.B: Malignant hypertension
options.C: Diabetic ketoacidosis
options.D: Addisonian crisis

explanation: You nailed it! Stopping steroids abruptly when the adrenal glands are inactive throws the body into a dangerous crash called an addisonian crisis. [learn more](GNS223_U5_T3#GNS223_U5_T3_h8)

question: Why must long-term steroid therapy be gradually tapered off instead of stopped overnight?

options.A: It gives the adrenal glands time to wake up and make natural hormones again.
options.B: It gives the liver time to clear leftover chemicals.
options.C: It keeps the original disease from coming back instantly.
options.D: It stops the patient from feeling sudden weight loss and fatigue.

explanation: Brilliant! Long-term steroids put the body's natural hormone factories (adrenals) to sleep. Tapering slowly wakes them back up safely. [learn more](GNS223_U5_T3#GNS223_U5_T3_h8)

question: What advice should a nurse give a patient taking oral prednisone to protect their stomach?

options.A: Take the medication on an empty stomach.
options.B: Crush the pills and dissolve them in juice.
options.C: Take the medication right before going to bed.
options.D: Take the medication with food or milk.

explanation: Correct! Steroids can be harsh on the gut lining, so taking them with food, milk, or a meal helps prevent stomach upset. [learn more](GNS223_U5_T3#GNS223_U5_T3_h9)

question: A patient on long-term steroid therapy asks why they need a medical alert bracelet. What is the best nursing response?

options.A: It proves to your insurance that you take your pills.
options.B: It warns people around you that you might gain weight.
options.C: It lets emergency staff know your adrenal glands are asleep if you have an accident.
options.D: It stops doctors from giving you new prescriptions.

explanation: Spot on! In an emergency, medical staff need to know your adrenal system is suppressed so they can provide extra steroid support your body can't make on its own. [learn more](GNS223_U5_T3#GNS223_U5_T3_h9)

question: What enzyme do NSAIDs block to lower pain and swelling?

options.A: Angiotensin-converting enzyme
options.B: Cyclooxygenase
options.C: Monoamine oxidase
options.D: Cholinesterase

explanation: Cyclooxygenase is the enzyme NSAIDs block to stop the body from making prostaglandins that cause inflammation. [learn more](GNS223_U5_T4#GNS223_U5_T4_h1)

question: Selective COX-2 inhibitors are designed to lower the risk of which common NSAID side effect?

options.A: Gastric mucosal ulceration
options.B: Peripheral edema
options.C: Respiratory depression
options.D: Hepatic failure

explanation: Because COX-1 protects the stomach lining, sparing it with selective COX-2 inhibitors helps prevent stomach ulcers. [learn more](GNS223_U5_T4#GNS223_U5_T4_h1)

question: Along with reducing pain and inflammation, what is the third main effect of NSAIDs?

options.A: Antimicrobial
options.B: Anticoagulant
options.C: Anticonvulsant
options.D: Antipyretic

explanation: Antipyretic drugs lower high body temperature by working on the part of the brain that controls body heat. [learn more](GNS223_U5_T4#GNS223_U5_T4_h2)

question: A student nurse is caring for a patient with severe menstrual cramps. Which drug class is best for initial pain relief?

options.A: Non-Steroidal Anti-Inflammatory Drugs
options.B: Loop diuretics
options.C: Inhaled beta-agonists
options.D: Broad-spectrum antibiotics

explanation: NSAIDs stop the body from making uterine prostaglandins, which are the main cause of cramping pain during menstruation. [learn more](GNS223_U5_T4#GNS223_U5_T4_h2)

question: Taking traditional NSAIDs for a long time most commonly damages which part of the body?

options.A: Gastrointestinal tract
options.B: Lymphatic system
options.C: Central nervous system
options.D: Endocrine system

explanation: Blocking COX-1 removes the stomach's natural protection, leaving the lining open to acid damage and ulcers. [learn more](GNS223_U5_T4#GNS223_U5_T4_h3)

question: Why can regular use of traditional NSAIDs lead to fluid swelling and high blood pressure?

options.A: Renal prostaglandin inhibition causes sodium and water retention
options.B: Vasodilation of peripheral arteries triggers fluid shifting
options.C: Direct stimulation of cardiac muscle increases stroke volume
options.D: Hepatic protein synthesis accelerates plasma osmolarity

explanation: When NSAIDs affect the kidneys, the body holds onto extra salt and water, leading to fluid buildup. [learn more](GNS223_U5_T4#GNS223_U5_T4_h3)

question: During which stage of pregnancy are standard NSAIDs strictly avoided?

options.A: First trimester
options.B: Entire duration of pregnancy
options.C: Third trimester
options.D: Second trimester

explanation: Using NSAIDs late in pregnancy can cause problems with the baby's heart blood vessels and complicate delivery. [learn more](GNS223_U5_T4#GNS223_U5_T4_h4)

question: Taking NSAIDs together with which type of drug creates a high risk of dangerous bleeding?

options.A: Bronchodilators
options.B: Thyroid hormones
options.C: Anticoagulants
options.D: Antifungals

explanation: Combining blood thinners with NSAIDs greatly increases the chance of serious stomach bleeding. [learn more](GNS223_U5_T4#GNS223_U5_T4_h4)

question: A patient with joint pain is prescribed diclofenac tablets. What advice should the nurse give to prevent stomach upset?

options.A: Crush the pill to speed up absorption
options.B: Swallow the tablet immediately before sleeping
options.C: Take the medication on an empty stomach
options.D: Take the medication with food or milk

explanation: Food or milk acts as a buffer so the drug does not irritate the stomach lining directly. [learn more](GNS223_U5_T4#GNS223_U5_T4_h5)

question: Which body check is most important before starting long-term NSAID therapy in an older patient?

options.A: Pulmonary function tests
options.B: Renal function tests
options.C: Fasteding blood glucose
options.D: Complete lipid profile

explanation: NSAIDs can reduce blood flow to the kidneys, making kidney function tests necessary before starting treatment. [learn more](GNS223_U5_T4#GNS223_U5_T4_h5)

question: What neurotransmitter is responsible for signal transmission at the neuromuscular junction?

options.A: Acetylcholine
options.B: Serotonin
options.C: Dopamine
options.D: Norepinephrine

explanation: Acetylcholine is the primary neurotransmitter released at the motor end-plate to stimulate muscle contraction. [learn more](GNS223_U5_T5#GNS223_U5_T5_h1)

question: Neuromuscular blocking agents cause muscle relaxation while having what primary effect on a patient's consciousness?

options.A: They lead to sudden loss of awareness
options.B: They cause deep general anesthesia
options.C: They leave consciousness completely unaffected
options.D: They induce profound sedation and amnesia

explanation: These drugs only block skeletal muscle movement and do not provide sedation, pain relief, or anesthesia. [learn more](GNS223_U5_T5#GNS223_U5_T5_h1)

question: Which drug acts as a depolarizing neuromuscular blocking agent?

options.A: Succinylcholine
options.B: Atracurium
options.C: Pancuronium
options.D: Rocuronium

explanation: Succinylcholine is the only widely used depolarizing neuromuscular blocker in routine clinical practice. [learn more](GNS223_U5_T5#GNS223_U5_T5_h2)

question: How do nondepolarizing neuromuscular blockers prevent skeletal muscle contraction?

options.A: By competitively occupying receptors without triggering depolarization
options.B: By depleting all stored acetylcholine inside the nerve terminal
options.C: By causing continuous electrical discharge within the muscle fibers
options.D: By destroying the enzyme acetylcholinesterase in the synapse

explanation: Nondepolarizing agents sit on the receptor sites and block acetylcholine from binding, preventing the muscle from receiving the signal to contract. [learn more](GNS223_U5_T5#GNS223_U5_T5_h2)

question: The primary reason neuromuscular blockers are given during rapid sequence intubation is to:

options.A: Provide optimal visualization of the vocal cords
options.B: Treat underlying bronchospasm in the airway
options.C: Lower the patient's systemic blood pressure
options.D: Induce rapid and profound unconsciousness

explanation: Relaxing the skeletal muscles of the pharynx and larynx allows safe and clear placement of the endotracheal tube. [learn more](GNS223_U5_T5#GNS223_U5_T5_h3)

question: A patient on a mechanical ventilator is actively fighting the machine settings despite heavy sedation. What class of medication is most appropriate to add?

options.A: Benzodiazepine
options.B: Opioid analgesic
options.C: Diuretic agent
options.D: Neuromuscular blocker

explanation: When sedation alone fails to control patient-ventilator dyssynchrony, neuromuscular blockers eliminate chest wall resistance and synchronize ventilation. [learn more](GNS223_U5_T5#GNS223_U5_T5_h3)

question: Which severe inherited condition can be triggered by the administration of succinylcholine?

options.A: Diabetic ketoacidosis
options.B: Malignant hyperthermia
options.C: Hepatic encephalopathy
options.D: Acute kidney injury

explanation: Succinylcholine is a known trigger for malignant hyperthermia in susceptible individuals, causing a rapid, life-threatening rise in body temperature. [learn more](GNS223_U5_T5#GNS223_U5_T5_h4)

question: Why is succinylcholine contraindicated in patients with severe, extensive burn injuries?

options.A: It induces prolonged and irreversible central nervous system depression
options.B: It completely fails to achieve adequate muscle relaxation
options.C: It accelerates the destruction of the healing skin grafts
options.D: It can cause dangerous increases in serum potassium levels

explanation: Upregulated receptors in burn patients can release massive amounts of potassium into the blood when exposed to succinylcholine, leading to cardiac arrest. [learn more](GNS223_U5_T5#GNS223_U5_T5_h4)

question: Neostigmine reverses nondepolarizing neuromuscular blockers by performing which action?

options.A: Inhibiting acetylcholinesterase to increase synaptic acetylcholine
options.B: Directly binding to and destroying the paralyzed muscle receptors
options.C: Chelating the circulating paralytic drug molecules in the bloodstream
options.D: Stimulating the release of stored calcium from the sarcoplasmic reticulum

explanation: By blocking acetylcholinesterase, neostigmine allows acetylcholine to accumulate and displace the nondepolarizing blocker from the receptors. [learn more](GNS223_U5_T5#GNS223_U5_T5_h5)

question: Why is an anticholinergic drug like atropine commonly administered alongside neostigmine?

options.A: To enhance the skeletal muscle tone of the recovering diaphragm
options.B: To prevent unwanted parasympathetic side effects such as severe bradycardia
options.C: To accelerate the renal excretion of the neuromuscular blocking agent

question: A client presents with rapid heart rate, dilated pupils, and severe agitation after taking an illicit pill. Which substance class is most likely responsible?

question: Why is establishing a non-judgmental relationship crucial during a substance use assessment?

question: How does nurse advocacy directly help a patient recovering from a substance use disorder?

question: What is another common name for first-generation antipsychotic drugs?

question: When should a patient take a rapid-acting insulin injection in relation to a meal?
